articles.title: Vendas de veículos novos têm melhor setembro da história, diz Fenabrave | G1
articles.standfirst: Emplacamentos somaram 509,7 mil unidades no mês, alta de 1,15% sobre agosto e de 8,32% na comparação anual.
articles.summary: Emplacamentos somaram 509,7 mil unidades no mês, alta de 1,15% sobre agosto e de 8,32% na comparação anual.
articles.body:
Carros circulam em São Paulo. — Foto: Alexandre Meneghini/Reuters

Os emplacamentos de carros, comerciais leves, caminhões e ônibus novos somaram 509.686 unidades em setembro, informou a Federação Nacional da Distribuição de Veículos Automotores (Fenabrave) nesta segunda-feira (5).

O número representa uma alta de 1,15% em relação a agosto. Esse foi o melhor resultado para um mês de setembro da série histórica. ; Na comparação com setembro do ano passado, os licenciamentos subiram 8,32%.

Já no acumulado do ano, as vendas somaram 4,23 milhões, aumento de quase 15% ante o mesmo período no ano passado.

As vendas de automóveis e comerciais leves cresceram 2,13% em relação ao mês anterior e 16,16% em relação ao ano anterior, somando 268.721. A expansão no principal segmento do setor, segundo o presidente da Fenabrave, Arcelio Junior, foi apoiada pela concorrência e por programas especiais de fomentação do setor, como o Move Brasil e Carro Sustentável.

"O mercado continua demonstrando demanda por veículos novos, mesmo em um ambiente ainda complexo de crédito", destacou.

A Fenabrave manteve as projeções para 2026, mas afirmou que elas poderão ser revisadas em novembro.

"Os resultados atuais nos indicam um fechamento de ano melhor do que o esperado, para a maior parte dos segmentos, mas vamos aguardar o desempenho de outubro, que pode apontar ajustes no mercado", acrescentou Arcelio Junior.

articles.title: Lula ganha em 165 cidades do RN e Flávio Bolsonaro em duas | G1
articles.standfirst: Dados gerais no Rio Grande do Norte mostram 59,7% dos votos - um total de 1,2 milhão - contra 34,7% de Flávio Bolsonaro, o que representou 720 mil votos.
articles.summary: Dados gerais no Rio Grande do Norte mostram 59,7% dos votos - um total de 1,2 milhão - contra 34,7% de Flávio Bolsonaro, o que representou 720 mil votos.
articles.body:
Mapa do RN: Lula ganhou em 165 cidades, Flávio em 2 — Foto: Arte g1

Candidato à reeleição, Lula (PT) teve mais votos à presidência da República em 165 das 167 cidades do Rio Grande do Norte neste domingo (4), no primeiro turno das eleições gerais.

As únicas exceções foram Parnamirim e Galinhos , onde Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) ficou à frente. Clique aqui para ver o Mapa da Apuração do g1, com dados por municípios.

Flávio Bolsonaro, que teve 47% dos votos, e Lula, que teve 45%, vão disputar o segundo turno das eleições no Brasil.

Em números gerais, Lula venceu no RN com 59,7% dos votos - um total de 1,2 milhão de votos - contra 34,7% de Flávio Bolsonaro, o que representou 720 mil votos.

Nas cidades em que venceu, Flávio Bolsonaro teve 50,9% dos votos contra 42,1% de Lula em Parnamirim e 48,3% contra 46,2% em Galinhos.

Em Natal , capital do estado e maior colégio eleitoral do Rio Grande do Norte, Lula venceu com 48,9% dos votos contra 44,1% de Flávio Bolsonaro. Em Mossoró, segundo maior colégio eleitoral, Lula teve 56,9% contra 36,1% de Flávio.

Os outros candidatos à presidência não venceram em nenhuma cidade do Rio Grande do Norte.

Flávio Bolsonaro ficou à frente de Lula em 14 estados e no Distrito Federal, enquanto Lula ganhou em 12 estados, incluindo os 9 do Nordeste.

articles.title: Congresso mais conservador: veja os desafios de Lula ou Flávio  | G1
articles.standfirst: Comentarista analisou no Bom Dia Brasil os possíveis cenários para o próximo governo diante da nova composição do Legislativo.
articles.summary: Comentarista analisou no Bom Dia Brasil os possíveis cenários para o próximo governo diante da nova composição do Legislativo.
articles.body:
O resultado do primeiro turno da eleição presidencial também definiu um novo cenário para o Congresso Nacional, que terá papel importante no próximo governo. Com uma composição mais conservadora, o Legislativo deve representar um desafio para os dois candidatos que seguem na disputa pela Presidência.

No Bom Dia Brasil desta segunda-feira (5), Miriam Leitão e Andréia Sadi analisaram como a composição do Congresso pode influenciar o próximo governo e destacaram, entre outros pontos, as dificuldades de governabilidade e a falta de renovação de parte das lideranças políticas.

Miriam Leitão avaliou que o Congresso eleito já tem uma característica mais conservadora e que os desafios serão diferentes dependendo de quem vencer a eleição presidencial.

Segundo a comentarista, em um eventual governo Lula, o presidente precisará usar sua capacidade de articulação para construir uma coalizão com o Centrão e garantir governabilidade. Para Miriam, essa tarefa tende a ser mais difícil diante de uma oposição forte.

"O presidente Lula, a menos que ele use toda a habilidade que já demonstrou no passado e construa uma coalizão, vai ter muito mais dificuldade. Acho que é o momento mais difícil para construir uma coalizão."

Miriam afirmou ainda que, nesse cenário, Flávio Bolsonaro teria uma oposição forte no Congresso.

Em um eventual governo de Flávio Bolsonaro, por outro lado, a comentarista avaliou que o cenário seria de tensão com as instituições. Segundo ela, o grupo político ligado ao candidato poderia tentar avançar sobre o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e promover mudanças que, na avaliação dela, enfraqueceriam as instituições.

"Ele começa pelo Supremo. Ele começa com essa questão que incomoda a sociedade, de fato, que vai ser fazer impeachment dos ministros do Supremo."

Para Miriam, a questão central seria, portanto, como garantir a governabilidade em um eventual governo Lula e como lidar com possíveis iniciativas de concentração de poder em um eventual governo Flávio Bolsonaro.

Andréia Sadi também analisou o resultado das eleições para o Congresso e chamou atenção para nomes tradicionais que ficaram de fora da próxima composição, especialmente na disputa por vagas no Senado.

Para Sadi, o resultado indica um desgaste de parte das lideranças tradicionais e uma demanda por renovação política.

"A impressão que a gente fica quando olha e faz a análise desses nomes que entraram e dos que ficaram de fora é que tem um cansaço das pessoas com essa falta de renovação também de caciques, principalmente nomes muito tradicionais da esquerda", afirmou.

Sadi disse ainda que candidatos do campo progressista tiveram dificuldades para renovar suas mensagens e construir palanques durante a campanha.

"Até conversando um pouco com a campanha do presidente Lula e algumas campanhas petistas, eles me diziam isso: que tiveram muita dificuldade de montar os palanques, primeiro, em alguns lugares, em algumas regiões importantes, e, segundo, em renovar os seus quadros."

Segundo a comentarista, esse movimento contrasta com o que ocorre no campo da direita, que apresentou nomes novos na disputa.

Miriam & Sadi: Lula teria dificuldades com Congresso e Flávio teria poder demais — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

articles.title: Socorro Neri é a deputada federal mais votada do Acre pela 2ª vez | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata do PP recebeu 39.587 votos nas eleições deste domingo (4) e agradeceu aos eleitores nas redes sociais. Professora e ex-prefeita de Rio Branco, ela seguirá para o 2º mandato em Brasília.
articles.summary: Candidata do PP recebeu 39.587 votos nas eleições deste domingo (4) e agradeceu aos eleitores. Professora e ex-prefeita de Rio Branco, ela seguirá para o 2º mandato em Brasília.
articles.body:
Socorro Neri (PP) é novamente a deputada federal mais eleita no Acre — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Socorro Neri ( PP ) foi reeleita deputada federal pelo Acre e, pela segunda vez consecutiva , terminou a eleição como a candidata mais votada para a Câmara dos Deputados no estado. ( Veja a lista completa dos oito parlamentares mais abaixo )

Com 100% das urnas apuradas, ela recebeu 39.587 votos, o equivalente a 8,45% dos votos válidos, nas eleições deste domingo (4).

Após a confirmação do resultado, a deputada publicou uma mensagem de agradecimento nas redes sociais onde afirmou que a votação representa o reconhecimento de pessoas que acompanharam o trabalho desenvolvido durante o primeiro mandato.

"Essa vitória é de cada pessoa que acreditou no nosso trabalho, caminhou ao nosso lado e confiou na força do bem coletivo. Seguiremos na Câmara dos Deputados com ainda mais força, coragem e compromisso com a nossa população", destacou.

Nascida em Tarauacá, no interior do Acre, Socorro Neri tem formação em pedagogia, mestrado e doutorado em Educação. Antes de ingressar na política, construiu a carreira acadêmica na Universidade Federal do Acre (Ufac), onde foi professora, pró-reitora e vice-reitora.

Também ocupou cargos na administração pública antes de chegar à Câmara. Foi secretária municipal de Assistência Social de Rio Branco , prefeita da capital, sendo a primeira mulher a ocupar o cargo , e secretária de Estado de Educação entre 2021 e 2022 .

Em 2022, foi eleita pela primeira vez para a Câmara dos Deputados e terminou aquela eleição como a deputada federal mais votada do Acre, com quase 26 mil votos.

Socorro Neri (PP) já foi vice-reitora da Ufac e prefeita de Rio Branco — Foto: Rafaela Rodrigues/g1

No primeiro mandato, iniciado em fevereiro de 2023, a atuação de Socorro Neri ficou concentrada principalmente nas áreas de educação, meio ambiente, direitos das mulheres e temas relacionados à Amazônia.

Ela chegou à Câmara como primeira vice-presidente da Comissão de Educação e também integrou a Comissão de Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Sustentável. Em 2023, também passou a ocupar a vice-presidência do Parlamento Amazônico e presidiu uma frente parlamentar voltada à transição climática justa.

Ao longo do mandato, participou de votações de projetos em diferentes áreas. Entre os registros da Câmara estão, por exemplo, votos favoráveis a propostas relacionadas à educação, economia, meio ambiente e legislação trabalhista, além de votações de urgência de projetos e medidas provisórias.

Em 2026, até o período registrado pela Câmara Federal antes da eleição, Neri havia participado de 125 votações nominais em plenário e apresentado 148 propostas, além de ter relatado 32 proposições, sendo a educação como uma das principais áreas de atuação.

Veja quem são os oito deputados federais eleitos no Acre em 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/g1

O Progressistas (PP) e o União Brasil foram os partidos que mais elegeram deputados federais, com dois cada. Em seguida, figuram MDB, Republicanos, PCdoB e PL, com 1 cada.

Em comparação com as Eleições de 2022, quatro candidatos foram reeleitos, 3 novos foram eleitos e uma retorna após já ter exercido mandato parlamentar, tendo uma renovação de 50%. Neste pleito, foram eleitas duas mulheres, diminuindo a quantidade, já que em 2022 três foram escolhidas.

articles.title: ‘If I didn’t write what moved me, it’d be like putting myself in prison’
articles.summary: Award-winning author Arundhati Roy discusses why she’s not afraid to address politically charged topics.
articles.body:
Since winning the Booker Prize in 1997 for her debut novel, author Arundhati Roy has not shied away from political issues. Whether she is writing fiction, nonfiction, or political essays, she focuses on social injustice.

The internationally acclaimed writer is an outspoken critic of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration. She describes India as a super poor nation, with a government that disempowers its citizens and silences dissent. Her activism goes beyond the pages of her books – she has also taken part in demonstrations against Modi’s policies. Supporters describe her as unrelenting in holding the political establishment to account. But critics accuse her of being divisive and anti-India. Despite what she calls scandal after scandal in the country, she is optimistic that political change is on the way.

articles.title: Miriam Leitão: Flávio e Lula precisam ir a debates no 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) agora terão uma nova etapa de campanha pela frente, com a necessidade de ampliar o diálogo com os eleitores e apresentar propostas para o país.
articles.summary: Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) agora terão uma nova etapa de campanha pela frente, com a necessidade de ampliar o diálogo com os eleitores e apresentar propostas para o país.
articles.body:
O primeiro turno da eleição presidencial terminou com a definição de dois candidatos para a disputa final. Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) agora terão uma nova etapa de campanha pela frente, com a necessidade de ampliar o diálogo com os eleitores e apresentar propostas para o país.

No Bom Dia Brasil desta segunda-feira (5), a comentarista Miriam Leitão avaliou que os dois candidatos precisam participar de debates e promover um confronto mais claro de ideias no segundo turno.

Segundo Miriam, faltou, ao longo do primeiro turno, um embate mais aprofundado entre os candidatos sobre propostas e os principais problemas do país.

"O que se espera é que tenha campanha, ou seja, que tenha debate. E, quando eu falo em debate, não estou falando apenas de um evento. Ao longo da campanha, não houve um embate de ideias."

Para Miriam, Lula precisa apresentar de forma mais clara quais serão suas propostas para os problemas enfrentados pelo governo, incluindo a situação fiscal e as contas públicas.

Ao mesmo tempo, ela avalia que Flávio Bolsonaro também precisa ser mais questionado sobre suas propostas e posições. Na avaliação da comentarista, o candidato não precisou, durante o primeiro turno, explicar de maneira mais detalhada como pretende governar e responder a questões relacionadas à democracia e a outros temas de sua campanha.

"Ele não precisou mostrar nada e não precisou se explicar sobre coisa nenhuma", afirmou Miriam.

Ela citou como exemplo o discurso de Flávio Bolsonaro após o resultado do primeiro turno, quando o candidato atribuiu ao governo atual a responsabilidade pelo recorde de feminicídios. Para Miriam, declarações como essa precisam ser confrontadas durante a campanha.

Para a comentarista, portanto, o segundo turno deve ser marcado por uma campanha mais efetiva dos dois candidatos — tanto nos debates quanto nas ruas.

"Flávio Bolsonaro e o presidente Lula têm que fazer campanha. Lula ficou muito no salto alto, como disse a Sadi, e ele tem que fazer campanha, tem que ir para a rua e tentar convencer o eleitor."

Miriam avalia ainda que os dois candidatos precisarão disputar especialmente os eleitores que não se sentiram representados pelas opções do primeiro turno e não foram votar.

"É preciso tentar convencer principalmente o eleitor que não foi votar porque não se sentia representado por nenhuma das duas forças políticas."

articles.title: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.summary: The student said she spoke with campus police in 2024 with what she believed was useful information about what was alleged at the Chi Phi fraternity house.
articles.body:
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.

The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.

The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had "gone off the rails," and she remembers being "really horrified by it."

"From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more," the student said.

Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity.

"The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn't handled," she said. "When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands."

The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8.

The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because "it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl." Doe's lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was "free p----" in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted.

"That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I'm taking this all in, and then I'm going to the police tomorrow," the student said.

She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police.

"They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me," she said.

She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept.

"I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn't enough," the student said.

Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student's account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations "deeply disturbing" and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm.

Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged "were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney." He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.

Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality.

Doe's suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten's handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe's allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter.

The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe's claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations.

Within Greek life at Cornell, "rumors spread fast," the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, "you knew someone who did."

Doe's lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.

Cornell said in a statement on Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions " from the university.

According to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled, and another two were suspected. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and "reflection papers."

Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men.

Chi Phi's national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.

"At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities," said Trey Robb, the national fraternity's interim executive director.

Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus.

Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News.

"We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them," said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe's lawsuit.

"As a team, it was important for us to support this victim," he said. "We are extremely, extremely distraught."

Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was "deeply disturbed" by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe.

"Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established," it said.

No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said.

As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe's sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News.

"Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn't know details," said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy.

Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as "really pissed off about it."

That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening.

A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, "and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment."

A third former Tri Delta member told NBC News that the campus learned of the incident from the university alert and described students feeling "shock" and "really appalled."

She, too, is critical of how Cornell handled the matter.

"I think that shows a lack of respect for their female students and kind of makes it less enticing to attend the university," she said.

Today, within the sorority there is a resounding wave of support for Doe, she said, as well as "frustration and anger."

Tri Delta said in a statement on behalf of its national organization and its Cornell chapter, "As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence."

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN's online chat service at .

articles.title: U.S. accuses California woman of spying for China, including surveilling Taiwan president’s son
articles.summary: U.S. authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — U.S. authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said. The FBI arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the agency said in a statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Zhang surveilled a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a U.S. resident. Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the U.S. government for protecting Taiwanese citizens. “Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement. China’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future. The Justice Department said Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family. Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement. It was not immediately clear whether Zhang has a defense attorney. She will appear on Monday in a Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said. Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the United States is the island’s most important international backer and ​weapons supplier.

articles.title: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez announces snap election amid housing crisis
articles.summary: Sanchez calls early vote after Parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
articles.body:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced a snap general election after Parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.

Sanchez said on Monday the vote would take place on November 29. “We need to renew people’s support,” he said in a televised address.

“We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in Parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”

In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.

The government said more than 70,000 people took part in a housing protest in the capital on Saturday.

For years, housing has been a top concern for Spaniards as current levels fall short of demand. According to real estate website Idealista, average rents have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent.

In his announcement, Sanchez acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of previous campaign promises.

“I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today,” Sanchez said.

But facing the electorate is a risky move for Sanchez. Opinion polls suggest that a coalition led by the conservative People’s Party (PP), with support from the far-right Vox party, is the most likely outcome in the election.

If they win, it will be the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco that a far-right party has entered central government.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged voters to bring his party to power in the election.

“The question I put to voters is whether they want four more years of what we’ve been living through, or whether they want to give change a chance,” he said in a televised address.

If Sanchez loses the election, it will also mark the end of one of Europe’s last left-leaning governments as the far right continues to gain ground across the continent.

Sanchez has stood out worldwide for his strong stance on progressive ideas, from defending the rights of Palestinian people to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on tech oligarchs.

The prime minister, who has never won enough votes to form a majority government, has brought together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, ranging from the far left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms, lasting eight years.

articles.title: Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation
articles.summary: The death of a worker at an anti-plague laboratory in Russia has prompted officials to put at least one hospital facility under quarantine and nearly 200 people reportedly under medical observation as of Monday.
articles.body: The death of a worker at an anti-plague laboratory in Russia has prompted officials to put at least one hospital facility under quarantine and nearly 200 people reportedly under medical observation as of Monday. The female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week, according to the regional governor, Igor Kobsev. He said no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body, and that there had been “no new cases” of illness among other employees of the lab. “The sanitary-epidemiological situation” in the area “is currently stable,” Kobsev said. On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation. Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been confirmed by officials. Meanwhile, there have been calls internationally for more information and greater transparency from Moscow. “Many details have not been confirmed,” a State Department spokesman said. “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.” The spokesman said there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that despite there being “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.” So the United States government is “watching and monitoring it closely,” he added. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it.” The World Health Organization said in a statement that it was aware of reports that a lab worker had died of “severe pneumonia” but that “no cause of death has been officially confirmed.” Asked by NBC News in Moscow whether the Kremlin was following these events, President Vladimir Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s consumer welfare service, was handling the investigation. “It is their official statements that should be relied upon— rather than paying heed to various rumors, speculations, and the like,” he said. “Rospotrebnadzor employs highly qualified professionals in this field, so let us heed their official statements.” Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News that “much more” information and transparency were needed from Moscow. He said that if this is an isolated case of pneumonic plague and no one else dies, “it will probably end there.” But “it’s actually very hard” for pneumonic plague to spread from person to person, Jha said. “We may see a few more people get infected, but the chances that this becomes a larger outbreak, let alone a global pandemic, is exceedingly low,” he said. “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me,” he said. “We need to understand that now.” The pneumonic plague is caused by the same bacteria as the bubonic plague and can spread from person to person through airborne respiratory droplets, typically from sneezing or coughing. Medical experts say cases require rapid treatment with powerful antibiotics to prevent fatalities. From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported more than 3,800 suspected human plague cases to the WHO, the agency said last week. Six of the countries ended up having confirmed cases, most of them in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, with 423 deaths.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un oversees AI missile launch; North Korea claims weapon holds manoeuvring capabilities
articles.summary: North Korea has claimed it has added artificial intelligence technology to a missile to make the weapon capable of changing its flight path and extremely
articles.body: North Korea has claimed it has added artificial intelligence technology to a missile to make the weapon capable of changing its flight path and extremely difficult to intercept, escalating concerns over Pyongyang's efforts to develop more sophisticated missile systems.North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the missile launch, with state media claiming the weapon demonstrated advanced manoeuvring capabilities, including flight at low altitude.Pyongyang claimed the weapon was fitted with an AI based guidance system that can make real time adjustments to its flight path, including low altitude manoeuvres, making it harder for enemy missile defence systems to predict and intercept.Kim's sister and senior North Korean official Kim Yo Jong said the missile demonstrated a “wave like” flight trajectory, which she claimed could complicate enemy tracking and interception.North Korea has presented the test as evidence of progress in developing weapons capable of penetrating advanced missile defence networks.North Korea described the weapon as an intermediate range strategic ballistic missile linked to its hypersonic strategic weapon system.According to South Korea, the missile was launched from the Wonsan area and travelled more than 700 km towards the East Sea. North Korean state media, however, claimed that it struck a target around 1,000 km away.South Korea's defence ministry said the missile was within the detection and interception capabilities of South Korean and US defence assets. It said the two allies maintain a strong combined defence posture and assessed that the weapon could be detected and intercepted.Why AI in missiles mattersThe significance of artificial intelligence in a missile lies less in simply making the weapon “smarter” and more in its potential to help the weapon process information and adjust its behaviour during flight.The Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) notes that hypersonic weapons combine high speed with manoeuvrability and relatively low-altitude flight, creating major challenges for conventional missile-defence systems. Unlike a traditional ballistic trajectory, a manoeuvring weapon can follow a less predictable path.That matters because missile defence depends heavily on detecting, tracking and predicting an incoming weapon's trajectory.CSIS says newer missile threats are increasingly flying lower, faster and on unpredictable trajectories, making them harder to detect and track and increasing the importance of advanced sensor networks.AI could potentially add another layer to this problem.The importance of AI in missiles is therefore not that it makes a weapon automatically “unstoppable”, but that AI-assisted guidance could potentially make a manoeuvring missile more adaptive and its trajectory harder for missile-defence systems to predict.

articles.title: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calls early election
articles.summary: Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November after recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
articles.body:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.

Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.

The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.

In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".

Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.

"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".

Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.

Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.

Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.

Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.

Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.

Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".

The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".

On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.

Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.

A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension.

She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.

Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home , but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.

The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.

The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".

The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.

The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.

Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.

In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.

She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.

In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.

And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

articles.title: Aberdare chapel from 19th Century goes for auction for £1
articles.summary: The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel was built in 1811, but is now overgrown and derelict.
articles.body:
A 19th Century revivalist chapel is going to auction with a guide price of just a £1.

The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel once held up to 900 worshippers but the building, with its long curved pews and high arched windows, was last used in 2009 and is now overgrown and derelict.

Paul Fosh Auctions said the "substantial detached property" in Aberdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had partial renovation work done but its planning permission for conversion to five flats had now lapsed.

"This large former chapel which also has a domestic-sized single garage is in the sought-after location of Trecynon," said auctioneer Sean Roper.

Roper said: "The Grade II listed chapel has two storeys of accommodation and sits in a sizeable but now overgrown plot with potential access from the front and rear of the site."

The site is about 0.23 acres and sits amid "well-established residential housing" about half a mile away from the town centre.

The property goes up for auction starting on 8 October.

articles.title: Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
articles.summary: After launching major military offensive to reclaim Houthi-held areas, Yemeni government says it has taken key district.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced a major military campaign to retake all territory controlled by the Houthis, marking a new escalation in a civil war that had largely been frozen for several years before battles intensified in recent weeks.

The announcement by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of the Yemeni government, comes after weeks of heavy fighting and major Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important city of Taiz.

On Monday, Yemeni government forces said they were launching a “strategic” offensive on the country’s capital, Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014.

Earlier in the day, the Yemeni forces — who are backed by Saudi Arabia — said they had regained control of the Dhubab district on the country’s west coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, though the Houthis denied the announcement.

The fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic – and Yemeni government forces has expanded since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing more than 100,000 people since then.

Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive that captured about 150km (93 miles) of Red Sea coastline and areas around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which is a critical route for international shipping.

On Monday, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally recognised government requested more support from the international community to defeat the Houthis, saying it is “in the world’s interest” for the country to be stable.

“We call upon our brothers, friends and the international community to support the Yemeni people, their state, and their national institutions in confronting the terrorist Houthi militia, which seizes their will by force of arms and lays waste to the lives of their sons – after exhausting all opportunities for de-escalation and peace,” Afrah al-Zouba said in a post on X.

So what is the latest on the fighting, and what does Yemen’s government hope to achieve?

The Yemeni government army said on Monday 1,747 Houthi fighters had been “neutralised” in 1,122 military operations in the Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates and along Yemen’s western coast.

Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted artillery and rocket positions, fortifications, supply lines, reinforcements and command centres.

Al-Nuzaili said warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers were involved and 364 military and logistical vehicles had been destroyed or disabled. The casualty and equipment figures could not be independently verified.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government also announced that its forces had taken control of Dhubab on the Red Sea coast and were launching a major offensive on Sanaa.

Elsewhere, the front line in Marib governorate in northeastern Yemen witnessed an escalation in fighting on Monday.

A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces launched an attack on Houthi positions on the Raghwan front in the north of the governorate, coinciding with air raids on Houthi positions and reinforcements.

The source said the raids targeted Houthi positions near Mount Helan as well as an arms depot and military reinforcements northwest of Marib.

On Sunday, a Saudi-led coalition said its forces carried out 97 attacks against Houthi reinforcements around Taiz and the Tor al-Baha front using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.

On the developments in Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau chief, Saeed Thabet, said Houthi operations in the rural areas around the strategic city are based on guerrilla tactics aimed at easing pressure on the coastal front and tightening the blockade of the road to Aden.

Al-Alimi said on Sunday that government forces had been ordered to launch military operations to regain Houthi-controlled territory and restore state authority across Yemen.

“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” al-Alimi said.

Military sources told the Reuters news agency that over the previous 48 hours, the Houthis advanced against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Taiz, pushing forward along the last remaining road linking the city with Aden on Yemen’s southern coast. The AFP news agency quoted four security sources as saying the Houthis had cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the Yemeni government’s interim capital.

The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen’s populous northwest since 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily the following year at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government but failed to dislodge the group.

A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought years of relative calm before fighting intensified again this year. The latest round of fighting has focused heavily on the Red Sea coast and Taiz.

Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni defence analyst, said he believes the government and its allies face a formidable rival in the Houthis.

The missile arsenal of the Houthis, the precision of their drones and military “capabilities have grown” with support from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), he told Al Jazeera.

Having joined the US-Israel war on Iran on their own timeline, the Houthis have reinforced their place in Tehran’s “axis of resistance” and given the IRGC a way to shift pressure from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea, he said.

Saudi Arabia has pledged continued support for the internationally recognised government.

Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia and its allies would continue supporting Yemen until state institutions were restored and the Houthi threat to shipping in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb was ended.

Al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia had an “inherent right” to defend its sovereignty and take military measures to deter Houthi offensives, citing attacks in Riyadh, Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran, Taif and Yanbu in recent weeks.

articles.title: Yemeni forces reclaim Dhubab, key positions near Bab al-Mandeb from Houthis
articles.summary: Army of internationally recognised gov’t claims key gains near strait before Saudi, Pakistani, Turkish officials meet.
articles.body:
The army of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has reclaimed control of the Dhubab district and key positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and also launched a “strategic offensive” on the capital Sanaa, a day after the government announced the launch of a major military operation against the Houthis.

“Forces from the Homeland Shield Forces and the Giants Brigades carried out a large-scale military operation with air cover targeting Houthi militia positions and movements in several areas of the district,” Yemen’s Saudi-backed military said in a statement carried by Yemen’s news agency Saba on Monday.

“During the operation, they advanced and seized important positions – cutting off supply lines and roads leading to Bab al-Mandeb,” an unnamed army source told Saba.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic, lost many fighters and several others were wounded in the clashes, with military equipment destroyed or damaged, according to the source.

Government forces are “continuing to comb and secure the liberated areas and cut off supply routes to the Houthi terrorist militia”, Saba reported.

Shortly after the announcement, the Saudi Arabia-led military coalition an air campaign was under way against the Houthis.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the Yemeni forces.

He said the coalition has secured “air protection” of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets.

Later, government forces announced the launch of a “strategic offensive” on Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, which has been controlled by the Houthis for more than a decade.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the battlefield reports.

Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the government to retreat to Aden.

The war escalated after a fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July.

In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines. On Sunday, ⁠⁠Rashad al-Alimi, the chairman of ⁠⁠Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, the executive body of the internationally recognised government, announced the start of military operations to retake the ⁠⁠remaining territory held by ⁠⁠the Houthis.

The battlefield reports come as Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar arrived in Saudi Arabia for a meeting with Saudi and Turkish officials under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement .

Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and military chief Asim Munir will accompany Dar at Monday’s talks in Riyadh with their counterparts from Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the Pakistani Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on X.

Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the defence pact on August 7 to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defence cooperation in the region. The pact stipulates that an attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on them all.

Pakistan’s Dar said last week the “ urgent talks ” would address a proposal for political engagement with the Iran-aligned Houthis as an alternative to the military option, following an approach by Tehran.

Al Jazeera’s Michael Appel said the Yemen war is expected to feature prominently in the Saudi-hosted talks.

“Civilians remain caught up in the fragmented front line of this war, and the announcement of an expanded military operation leaves tens of thousands with the prospect of continued displacement and hunger as a humanitarian crisis takes hold,” he said.

articles.title: The Supreme Court is back. These five cases could reshape American life
articles.summary: From climate lawsuits and second amendment rights to election integrity, five Supreme Court cases could reshape major constitutional battles this term.
articles.body: The Supreme Court begins its new term on Monday. The justices have filled only part of their docket, with more cert grants still to come. It is not too early to predict another good term for defenders of the Constitution, thanks to an originalist majority that takes its text and history seriously. Here are five cases to watch closely. 1. Climate lawfare: Suncor Energy v. Commissioners of Boulder County The term opens with a case that could end one of the left’s most brazen lawfare campaigns — or drive prices at the pump even higher. Boulder, Colorado, is suing Suncor and ExxonMobil in state court under Colorado tort law, seeking gargantuan damages for the effects of global climate change. In other words, Boulder wants Colorado law to punish these companies for emissions in every state and around the world. Dozens of states and cities have filed similar suits. An outside counsel for Boulder’s legal team has publicly described such climate litigation as effectively imposing a "carbon tax" and acknowledged that it could raise fossil-fuel prices and potentially push energy companies toward bankruptcy. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Having failed to win their policy argument in Congress, activists are hoping they will have more success in friendly state courts. The principal question for the justices is whether federal law bars these claims; the court will also consider whether it has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear the case. It does. For more than a century, the court has treated emissions that cross state lines as a federal issue. The Clean Air Act includes provisions that allow a state to regulate pollution sources within its borders, but sources outside them are a different matter, as the court previously held in a case involving nearly identical Clean Water Act provisions. Underneath all of this is a basic structural principle: The Constitution treats the states as equals, and none may govern beyond its own borders. A clear reversal would check every state or municipality that tries to set national policy in defiance of the structural Constitution. 2. There Colorado goes again: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy Colorado promised every family in the state free preschool at the school of its choice, public or private. Then it shut out Catholic preschools because they support Church teaching on sex and gender. In testimony highlighted by the Catholic schools, the program’s director said hypothetically that a participating preschool could seek preferences for "gender-nonconforming children" or members of "the LGBTQ community," provided the preference complied with the program’s nondiscrimination requirements. That double standard is the antithesis of neutrality and a constitutional nonstarter. The court has considered similar discriminatory systems in recent years and has struck them down every time. SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION Three times since 2017 — in cases from Missouri, Montana and Maine — the court has ruled that the government cannot exclude people of faith from public benefits because of their religion. Colorado itself has lost three major First Amendment cases for showing hostility to a baker’s faith (Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, 2018), threatening to force a web designer to create wedding websites against her beliefs (303 Creative LLC v. Elenis, 2023), and censoring a Christian counselor’s viewpoint in talk therapy while permitting the opposite one (Chiles v. Salazar, 2026). The smart money is on another Colorado loss. 3. Second Amendment: Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins The court consolidated two cases for argument asking whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments protect the right to own an AR-15, the most popular rifle in America. Viramontes challenges Cook County, Illinois’ ban on so-called "assault weapons," and Grant challenges a similar Connecticut law. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS These cases will be a showcase for originalist interpretation. Under District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) and New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022), the Second Amendment protects arms in common use for lawful purposes, and a ban survives only if the state can point to historical analogues showing it fits the nation’s tradition of firearm regulation. This will be an opportunity for the Supreme Court to clarify how to determine which weapons are protected as "arms" and how common they must be to be part of the right to keep and bear arms. 4. Election integrity: Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota Arizona passed laws in 2022 requiring documentary proof of citizenship from people who register to vote using the state’s form and allowing officials to remove confirmed noncitizens from the rolls as a federal election approaches. The Ninth Circuit blocked both provisions as preempted by the National Voter Registration Act. It also found the proof-of-citizenship requirement to be barred by a 2018 consent decree settling a lawsuit by left-wing advocacy groups, in which a former secretary of state agreed to register applicants who submitted no proof of citizenship as "federal-only" voters. THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA This case presents quite a spectacle: Arizona’s opponents will stand before the Supreme Court and argue that federal law forces a state to keep people it knows are noncitizens on its voter rolls. And part of their case rests on rules no elected representative ever passed. That decree lets a single official’s settlement do what only the legislature should, handing activists something with the force of law. Left standing, arrangements like this can cause mischief well beyond Arizona. 5. Parental rights: International Partners for Ethical Care v. Ferguson Parental rights keep returning to the court, and this case illustrates why. Washington amended its runaway-youth-shelter law so that when a minor is seeking so-called "gender-affirming" services, shelters no longer have to notify the parents. Instead, they notify only the state, giving the parents the type of treatment normally reserved for abusers. The state may then keep them from locating their child and delay reunification until they accept the state’s approach. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The immediate question before the court is standing — whether these parents can sue at all because their gender-confused children, thankfully, have not yet run away. But parents are already affected by the new law, walking on eggshells, knowing the state would take their children’s side against them. The Ninth Circuit dismissed that harm as speculative and self-inflicted. But parents should not have to wait until a child disappears or undergoes irreversible procedures before they can defend their rights in court. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With so many important issues riding on this term’s decisions — from climate lawfare and religious liberty to gun rights and election integrity — it is a relief to know that they will be heard by an originalist Court. And with the court set to grant even more cases on Monday, this is only the beginning. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM CARRIE CAMPBELL SEVERINO

articles.title: The Republican consensus on Israel is starting to fracture
articles.summary: Christian Zionism made support for Israel a Republican cause. America First Republicans are challenging that consensus.
articles.body:
The Republican Party’s powerful alliance with Israel — repeatedly reaffirmed during President Donald Trump’s second term — is rooted in conservative Christianity’s rise as a political force more than half a century ago.

The Reverend Billy Graham’s relationship with President Richard Nixon helped bring evangelical politics into the White House. Graham later regretted his political entanglement, particularly after Watergate, but the opening remained. In the late 1970s, Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority mobilised conservative evangelicals into a potent Republican constituency that Ronald Reagan incorporated into his conservative coalition. Israel became increasingly central to that identity, with many evangelicals viewing support for the Jewish state through a biblical rather than purely strategic lens. Leaders such as televangelist John Hagee and Christians United for Israel later built an institutional network that translated religious conviction into political pressure. What began as evangelical access to Republican presidents became a durable political infrastructure.

For Christian Zionists, this alliance is about more than religious affinity. Many view Israel as central to biblical prophecy, including end-times interpretations and the anticipated return of Jesus Christ. These beliefs elevated support for Israel from a foreign-policy preference to a religious commitment. As evangelical voters became a core Republican constituency, politicians had strong electoral incentives to embrace that commitment, bringing theology, party loyalty and strategic interests into closer alignment.

Today’s Republican leaders inherited that system.

Mike Johnson of Louisiana, the speaker of the US House of Representatives, embodies its contemporary influence. He has invoked biblical passages to portray the relationship between the US and Israel as more than a conventional strategic partnership. His speakership gives him considerable influence over legislation, congressional spending and debates over US military assistance to Israel.

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas has repeatedly framed his support for Israel in explicitly Christian terms. Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas represents a more nationalist, hawkish version of the alliance. His effort to replace “West Bank” with “Judea and Samaria” in federal terminology illustrates how biblical language can enter government policy.

Former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee, now Trump’s ambassador to Israel, represents the same intersection of evangelical Christianity and Republican politics. His defence of Israeli settlements and rejection of conventional territorial terminology reflect a worldview in which biblical claims carry substantial political weight.

These figures did not create the alliance; they are its current custodians. Their influence extends beyond rhetoric. Congressional votes on military assistance, diplomatic protection and sanctions translate political commitments into policy. Christian Zionist organisations sustain that influence through church networks, lobbying, grassroots mobilisation and direct engagement with elected officials, keeping their priorities prominent even when other Republicans question overseas commitments.

Trump and the America First complication

President Donald Trump strengthened the evangelical alliance with Israel while introducing a competing force into Republican foreign policy: America First.

His administration’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and relocation of the US embassy fulfilled a longstanding Christian Zionist priority. Yet Trump’s coalition also includes voters sceptical of foreign entanglements, overseas military interventions and extensive foreign assistance. This creates a tension within the Republican consensus.

For Christian Zionists, support for Israel can constitute a biblical obligation. For some America First Republicans, the question is whether that commitment advances a clearly defined American interest. The positions overlap but are not identical.

The tension sharpens when support for Israel risks a wider war, additional deployments or prolonged US involvement in the Middle East. The Iran war has exposed precisely this contradiction, forcing Republicans to confront the point at which support for Israel collides with America First opposition to prolonged military involvement abroad. Religious conservatives may regard biblical commitments as decisive while more isolationist Republicans question the financial costs, potential American casualties and responsibilities Washington assumes on behalf of other countries.

Trump has sought to accommodate both constituencies, but their competing priorities have become increasingly difficult to reconcile.

A more consequential challenge may be emerging among younger Republicans.

A Pew Research Center March survey found that Republicans overall viewed Israel more favourably than unfavourably, by 58 percent to 41 percent. Among Republicans aged 18 to 49, however, 57 percent held unfavourable views. Older Republicans remained substantially more favourable. A separate Pew survey in May found that 42 percent of Republican-leaning Americans aged 18 to 29 viewed Israelis favourably, compared with 83 percent of those aged 65 and older. Although the surveys measured different populations and questions, both revealed a pronounced generational divide.

These findings do not mean younger Republicans have abandoned Israel or oppose the US-Israel relationship. They do suggest that the constituency underpinning the alliance is becoming less uniform.

The reasons extend beyond ideology. Younger Americans encounter the conflict through social media, reporting on Gaza and images of civilian suffering. Some question whether religiously grounded foreign-policy commitments serve American interests. Others support Israel while opposing particular Israeli government policies. Unfavourable views of Israel should not automatically be equated with hostility towards Israelis or rejection of the bilateral relationship.

Nevertheless, a generation increasingly divided over Israel may prove less receptive to appeals treating support for the country as an unquestionable test of conservative identity.

Israel has developed into more than a foreign-policy priority. For millions of conservatives, support for Israel has been part of the Republican Party’s religious and moral identity.

That legacy remains powerful, but its foundations are shifting. Younger Republicans came of age during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump’s nationalism, scepticism towards foreign intervention and Israel’s war on Gaza. Their questions increasingly concern not only theology but also national interests: What does US support for Israel accomplish, what does it cost and when should religious conviction yield to strategic considerations?

Such questions may reshape the coalition without immediately dismantling it. Evangelical organisations retain substantial resources, access to political leaders and the capacity to mobilise voters. Their congressional allies hold positions of considerable influence, and changing public opinion does not automatically translate into new party platforms or congressional votes.

Yet the growing divide between older evangelical voters and younger Republicans presents a longer-term challenge. Christian Zionism succeeded so thoroughly that its premises became Republican orthodoxy. But an alliance sustained by religious conviction, institutional influence and partisan loyalty becomes harder to preserve when a new generation questions those underlying assumptions.

For decades, support for Israel could be presented simultaneously as foreign policy and faith. Increasingly, younger Republicans may demand a different justification, one grounded in demonstrable US interests rather than religious obligation alone. Whether Republican support for Israel can survive that shift may become a defining test of the party’s evolving identity.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 3 scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine for work unraveling the brain’s mysteries
articles.summary: Three scientists won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine Monday for discoveries that allow researchers to switch on and off nerve cells in the living brain.
articles.body: STOCKHOLM — Three scientists won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine Monday for discoveries that allow researchers to switch on and off nerve cells in the living brain. Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Peter Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners. Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said. “This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.” The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days. The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel‘s will and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited interruptions, chiefly during World War I and World War II. A sixth award, the economics prize, was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, the Riksbank. The medicine prize has honored some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past century, including Alexander Fleming’s work on penicillin, recognized in 1945, and Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups. Last year, American scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan’s Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer. Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in Oslo, a tradition often linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel‘s lifetime. More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their long-standing traditions. The celebrations culminate Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel‘s death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honor.

articles.title: Egypt’s earliest kings were buried with hundreds of servants; 100 years later, skull fractures are reviving the theory that some were sacrificed
articles.summary: Skull fractures found on remains from the royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos suggest that servants of Egypt’s earliest kings may have been
articles.body: Skull fractures found on remains from the royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos suggest that servants of Egypt’s earliest kings may have been sacrificed when their rulers died. A new study by bioarchaeologist Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, published on 5 October 2026 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology and reported by Nicola Davis in The Guardian, re-examined skulls first excavated a century ago. Eighteen of forty-six skulls showed injuries consistent with death around the time of burial. The findings appear to support a theory proposed by the pioneering Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, though the evidence remains incomplete.How forensic bioarchaeology reexamined skulls from the First Dynasty royal cemetery at Abydos, EgyptAccording to the study ‘New data from old bones: using bioarchaeology and forensics to reassess legacy data from ancient Abydos, Egypt’ in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, the royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab holds the tombs and funerary enclosures of the First Dynasty kings, who ruled roughly five thousand years ago. Around those structures lie hundreds of smaller graves, which scholars believe belonged to court officials, craftspeople and other members of the royal household. The Guardian reports that these graves also include people described as ladies, seal-bearers and inspectors.Flinders Petrie excavated many of these graves in the 1920s. Campbell tracked down forty-six skulls from the graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of King Djer, King Djet and Queen Merneith. They are held in the Duckworth Collection at the University of Cambridge. Campbell told The Guardian that the question of retainer sacrifice has been debated for more than a century, but that hers is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves.Eighteen of forty-six crania exhibit potentially lethal fractures and one injury to the eyeCampbell reports that eighteen of the forty-six skulls, about thirty-nine per cent, showed injuries from around the time of death. The most common were linear fractures across the top of the skull. There were also several sharp-force injuries, including a wound that penetrated the side of the head and a chopping injury to the eye. Campbell explains in the paper that linear fractures of this kind often cause bleeding inside the skull, which can lead to unconsciousness and death without surgery.The injuries do not match the famous image of a king smashing enemies with a mace. A stone mace would have caused depressed fractures, which are dents in the bone. Instead, the linear fractures are more consistent with flat, wide objects made of wood or antler. The paper also notes that injuries above the line where a hat brim would sit tend to come from deliberate blows rather than accidental falls.Why Flinders Petrie missed the evidence of human sacrifice during his excavations of the royal tombsPetrie suspected that so many people could not have died naturally at the same time, yet he reported no signs of trauma on the bones. He even suggested that some individuals might have been stunned and buried alive. Campbell argues that Petrie probably did see the cracks but took them for damage caused by the burial environment over time. As evidence, she points to the paraffin wax he applied to stabilise the skulls, which often surrounds the fractures.Modern forensic science can tell injuries made around the time of death from damage made long afterwards, because fresh bone breaks differently from dry bone. The study also finds that the way the skeletons lay does not clearly support burial alive. It further finds that the well-preserved small bones of the hands and feet argue against the theory that the bodies were moved from earlier graves.What experts say about retainer sacrifice and the limits of such a small skull sampleCampbell is careful about what the evidence can prove. She told The Guardian that for skulls without trauma, sacrifice cannot be confirmed, and that some retainers may have been sacrificed while others were not. The surviving skulls are only a small fraction of the original burial populations, which the study estimates at between five and fifteen per cent at each enclosure. Many of the other bones were lost or reburied together.Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, also welcomed the idea, saying the idea was not entirely new but that the paper is one of the few to apply rigorous current methods to these remains. She suggested that some retainers might have welcomed an eternal life serving a god-king, while others could have been terrified and tried to escape. Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University in Alabama, said similar sacrifices happened in other cultures and eras, and that such scenes would have been very gruesome. She added that not everyone may have gone willingly.Why the practice ended so quickly in later Egyptian tombsThe number of servant graves around royal tombs dropped quickly and seems to disappear with the start of the Second Dynasty, according to Campbell. Ikram told The Guardian the practice was short-lived because people were replaced by statuettes in later periods.Campbell’s paper places the finding in a wider context. At the royal cemetery of Ur in ancient Mesopotamia, modern computed tomography scans overturned an earlier belief that attendants had peacefully drunk poison, revealing severe blunt force injuries to the skull instead. At Kerma in Nubia, researchers found no clear trauma but still considered sacrifice the most likely explanation. The Abydos study argues that other long-stored excavation collections deserve fresh examination with modern methods.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
