articles.title: Former Prince Andrew launches challenge to ‘quash’ police search warrants
articles.summary: A London court is likely to hold a private hearing on Thursday as Mountbatten-Windsor challenges Thames Valley Police.
articles.body:
Former British Prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched a High Court challenge to “quash search warrants” obtained by the police before his arrest earlier this year.

The judiciary confirmed on Monday that a London court is likely to hold a private hearing on Thursday as Mountbatten-Windsor challenges Thames Valley Police over searches of his former homes on royal estates.

The disgraced royal was arrested on February 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that he shared sensitive information with the late American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein during his time as the United Kingdom’s trade envoy.

While he was released later that day, the 66-year-old remains under investigation. Mountbatten-Windsor has denied wrongdoing.

Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal titles last year following his connections to Epstein, who died in a prison in New York, United States, in August 2019.

Officers searched Mountbatten-Windsor’s home on the remote Sandringham royal estate in eastern England and his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, west of London.

The judiciary’s press office said the case concerned an application by Mountbatten-Windsor for a “judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on February 18, 2026”.

It said Thursday’s hearing was about an application by Thames Valley Police to restrict access to court documents in the matter.

“Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court,” the police said in a statement.

“As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ruling BJP on Monday said the Supreme Court's decision to issue notices to the Election Commission (EC) and the Centre on pleas seeking the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ruling BJP on Monday said the Supreme Court's decision to issue notices to the Election Commission (EC) and the Centre on pleas seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar showed that all institutions in the country were "functioning independently" and there was no atmosphere of "fear and dictatorship"."The country is moving in a very democratic way. Everyone is speaking their heart out. All procedures and systems are being followed. Where else could there be a better model of democracy? I feel India is celebrating democracy," BJP MP and spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters at a news conference at the party headquarters in Delhi when asked about the development.Also Read | SC seeks EC response on changes during SIR: Why has Form 6 become a flashpoint — explainedPatra's remarks came after the Supreme Court sought responses from the EC and the Centre within a week on a plea challenging the manner in which the poll panel, led by CEC Gyanesh Kumar, allegedly took decisions without the approval of the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.However, a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to pass any interim order in the matter.The bench observed that it could not pass an order merely on the basis of a media report, which may or may not be accurate. However, it asserted that if any decisions of the EC were found to have been taken unilaterally by the CEC, the Supreme Court could reconsider or recall them."They (EC) are expected to take unanimous decisions. If there is no unanimity, it has to be by majority. If records show some decision was not unanimous, etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra vires. Can we ex parte come to a decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner," the CJI said.The controversy stems from an Indian Express report published late last month, which claimed that Sandhu and Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The report alleged that some of these decisions were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.Also Read | 'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotesAccording to the report, the poll panel's ECINet software added a requirement for ancestral details and a link to the previous SIR in Form 6, the voter registration form, without the legal amendment required under election rules. The two commissioners reportedly objected to the change.The EC has since restored Form 6 to its original format in states where the SIR has been completed. However, the requirement continues in states and Union territories where the roll revision is still underway.Responding to the Indian Express report, the commission said that "differing views and observations" among its members were a "normal part" of deliberations in any multi-member institution. The EC also stated that all decisions, including those related to the SIR, were taken unanimously by Kumar and the two Election Commissioners.Rahul Gandhi ups the ante against CECMeanwhile, Congress MP and Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi upped the ante against Kumar after the Supreme Court clarified that it did not approve any modification made by the EC in Form 6.In a social media post on X, the Congress leader accused the CEC of changing the application citizens use to register as new electors "illegally and unilaterally."Also Read | 'CEC changed Form 6 illegally, unilaterally': Rahul Gandhi ups the ante after SC's clarification"It is now established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally. This is just one more proof of him abusing his position to help the BJP," Rahul Gandhi wrote on X, adding that was now established "beyond doubt" that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 "illegally and unilaterally."He also shared the screenshot of the September 26 Election Commission statement which read -- "The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. articles.title: Pennsylvania data centre developer offers 4,500 households $10,000 each; residents refuse, saying money isn't enough
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania developer is offering an unusually large financial incentive to win support for a proposed artificial intelligence data centre campus, but
articles.body: A Pennsylvania developer is offering an unusually large financial incentive to win support for a proposed artificial intelligence data centre campus, but many residents say the money is not worth the potential cost to their community. NorthPoint Development has proposed Project Hazelnut, a data centre campus covering roughly 1,300 acres in Hazle Township, in the Pocono foothills. As part of a broader community-benefits package, the company says about 4,500 eligible households would each receive $10,000 if the project is approved and reaches the required stage. That would put the direct household fund at about $45 million. Despite the offer, residents have raised concerns about noise, light pollution, property values, energy demand, water use and the long-term impact of the development.NorthPoint's $10,000 offer to residentsNorthPoint announced its direct resident grant programme as part of a wider package linked to Project Hazelnut. The company says it has set aside $45 million to provide $10,000 to every eligible Hazle Township household. Residents would be free to use the money as they choose, although NorthPoint says it could help with home maintenance, improvements, landscaping or solar projects. Importantly, the payment is conditional on the project moving forward. According to NorthPoint's project FAQ, the $10,000 would be paid when the certificate of occupancy is issued for the first data centre building, which the company currently anticipates could happen in late 2027.The proposed campus could have 15 buildingsProject Hazelnut is planned as a large-scale data centre campus near Humboldt Industrial Park. NorthPoint's proposal covers approximately 1,280 to 1,300 acres and could eventually include as many as 15 data centre buildings. The developer says the project would bring construction and permanent employment, new tax revenue and infrastructure investment to the area. NorthPoint has also promoted environmental measures, including preserving large portions of the property as forest and open space and designing the facility to avoid using local drinking water for cooling. These claims come from the developer and should be distinguished from independently established impacts because the project has not yet been approved or built.The offer is part of a much larger packageThe $45 million household fund is only one part of NorthPoint's proposed community benefits. The company's current plan describes a total commitment of $165 million. That includes $15 million for community programmes such as workforce development, education, arts, recreation and youth initiatives, plus another $105 million over 15 years. NorthPoint says the latter would provide Hazle Township with up to $7 million a year that could be used for local services, including establishing a police department and reducing residents' trash fees. The developer previously announced a $30 million community development fund aimed partly at offsetting potential short-term local utility-rate increases, but its later proposal expanded the overall community-benefit commitment.Why residents remain opposedFor many opponents, the central issue is not simply whether $10,000 is a significant amount of money. Residents interviewed about the proposal have questioned whether a one-time payment can compensate for potential long-term changes to the area. Concerns include construction and operational noise, light pollution, possible effects on property values, increased energy demand and the broader environmental footprint of a major data centre campus. Some residents have described the payments as resembling a bribe, while others have argued that the potential effect on nearby homes could outweigh the financial benefit. At the same time, the offer has not been universally rejected, and some residents acknowledge that $10,000 would be substantial for local households.The project still faces major legal hurdlesThe proposed campus is far from construction. Hazle Township supervisors rejected NorthPoint's land-development application in November 2025. The proposal was for a 15-building data centre complex on roughly 1,280 acres. In June 2026, a Luzerne County judge denied an appeal by NP Hazleton Logistics, a NorthPoint affiliate, and said the developer could pursue approval through the township's zoning hearing board because the existing zoning ordinance did not specifically address data centres. The township subsequently declared parts of its zoning ordinance invalid for failing to address data centres and imposed a limited 180-day moratorium while officials worked on new regulations. NorthPoint's legal challenge and the zoning process therefore remain important obstacles to the project.Pennsylvania is tightening data centre rulesThe dispute comes as Pennsylvania itself is imposing tougher requirements on large data centre projects. On August 18, 2026, Governor Josh Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05, establishing the state's Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, requirements. Under the order, the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection will review qualifying data centre permit applications only after developers make legally binding commitments to meet the requirements and obtain necessary local approvals. The rules address energy affordability, environmental protection, water use, transparency, local hiring and community benefits. The administration also removed data centres from the state's Fast Track permitting programme and prohibited the use of nondisclosure agreements for data centre projects.The wider fight over AI infrastructureHazle Township's dispute reflects a broader US debate over where the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure should be built and who should pay for it. Data centres can bring construction work, permanent jobs and tax revenue, but communities have increasingly questioned their demands for electricity, water and land. articles.title: After 47 years of confronting Iran, does America have a strategy for ending this war?
articles.summary: Trump told the United Nations Iran must make a deal or face destruction, but seven months of war have yet to produce a clear political end state.
articles.body: President Donald Trump stood before the United Nations and presented Iran with a choice: reach an agreement that would allow the country to rebuild or face the destruction of the Islamic Republic. The following day, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian rejected surrender while leaving the door open to negotiations. More than seven months into the war, Washington still has not answered the question that has dogged American policy since 1979: What political outcome is America trying to achieve, and how will military force bring it about? I was an Army officer serving in West Germany when Iranian militants seized our embassy in Tehran on Nov. 4, 1979. Fifty-two Americans endured 444 days of captivity. That crisis began a hostile relationship that has outlasted eight American presidents. TRUMP KEEPS NEGOTIATING WHILE IRAN PLAYS THE LONG GAME AMERICA KEEPS MISSING In April 1988, after USS Samuel B. Roberts struck an Iranian mine, President Ronald Reagan authorized Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, American forces sank two Iranian ships and wrecked two surveillance platforms. Yet the confrontation continued. The 2015 nuclear agreement sought to constrain Tehran through negotiated restrictions and international inspections. Trump withdrew from that agreement in 2018 and restored economic sanctions. Neither approach settled the wider confrontation. TRUMP’S IRAN WAR NOW COMES DOWN TO ONE BRUTAL QUESTION: WHAT COMES NEXT? Trump went much further. American strikes in June 2025 hit three key nuclear facilities. Then, on Feb. 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury, beginning the current war. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei died on the first day. Seven months later, Iran has sustained extensive military losses, as Trump emphasized in his Sept. 22 U.N. address. But damaging Iran’s forces is not the same as achieving the campaign’s political objectives. TRUMP HAS 3 CHOICES TO DEFINE VICTORY IF HE WANTS TO BEAT IRAN. NONE OF THEM ARE EASY As a retired Army officer and former Pentagon strategist, I spent much of my career on the relationship between military operations and national objectives. Destroying an adversary’s forces is a military result. Victory is the political outcome those operations were meant to produce. Nowhere does that distinction matter more than in Iran. THREE CHOICES NOW DEFINE TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AND ALL OF THEM HAVE A COST What is the Trump administration trying to accomplish? Secretary of War Pete Hegseth put it bluntly in March: "no nukes, no navy, and a complete dismantling of their missile program and defense industrial base." Reopening the Strait of Hormuz joined the list later. The administration has never explicitly declared regime change a goal, yet the president now speaks of destroying the Islamic Republic. Those are military tasks, not a political end state, and even the nuclear goal has wavered. In April, Trump said of Iran’s buried uranium, "I don’t care about that." Two weeks later he promised, "We’re going to take it." IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY That matters because America has lost its best window into Iran’s program. Until Feb. 28, International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors were still working inside Iran, and the agency was tracking activity at the Isfahan tunnels where Tehran stored much of its enriched uranium. Iran had barred inspectors from the sites bombed in June 2025, but the agency still had eyes in the country. Since the war began, inspectors have been unable to visit any nuclear facility except the Bushehr power plant. Destroying an adversary’s forces is a military result. Victory is the political outcome those operations were meant to produce. Before the June 2025 strikes, the agency estimated Iran held 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched to 60%, enough for about 10 weapons if refined further. The IAEA cannot verify where that material is today. On September 9, the agency’s board referred Iran to the U.N. Security Council. Without inspectors, no one can confirm what the bombing achieved. AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS Beyond the bomb, the political objective is murkier. Is Washington trying to change how the regime behaves, or to end the regime itself? Those are different wars. Changing a government’s conduct requires defined concessions and a means of verifying them. Replacing a government requires knowing who governs afterward. Iraq taught that lesson: defeating Saddam Hussein’s military proved far easier than establishing a durable political order. IRAN REGIME CHANGE TALK RESURFACES AS TRUMP SAYS TEHRAN 'WANTS TO MEET' AMID US STRIKES The Islamic Republic remains in power. Reuters reported in April that the Revolutionary Guards had tightened their grip on military strategy and major political decisions. The war has strengthened the institution most committed to continuing it. Time favors Tehran. Iran’s leadership is prepared for a prolonged confrontation, while American presidents depend on public support, and that support is thin. IRAN ‘MISCALCULATING’ BY BETTING ON MIDTERMS AFTER 3-HOUR TALKS, TRUMP OFFICIALS WARN Americans who lived through the Cold War needed no briefing on the Soviet threat. Thousands of nuclear warheads were aimed at our cities. Iran’s threat is harder to see. The administration first cited an imminent danger, then shifted its rationale more than once. A June Reuters/Ipsos survey found that only 24% of Americans considered the war worth its costs. In July, most said Trump had not clearly explained its objectives. What Americans do understand is the price at the pump. Gasoline topped $4 a gallon in April for the first time since 2022, and AAA’s national average is about $4.43 today. The Strait of Hormuz helps explain why. Oil flows through the strait fell from 21.6 million barrels per day late last year to 4.9 million this spring. Crude shipments have since rebounded to near prewar levels, but shipments of refined fuels such as gasoline and diesel remain far below their prewar volume, helping keep fuel prices elevated. Trump himself told the U.N. he believes Iran is waiting for the November midterm results before making a deal. On Sept. 29, the Revolutionary Guards issued a 25-page open letter urging American voters to reject Trump’s policies. Tehran is working the American home front. Renewed negotiations have exposed the gaps. Tehran has proposed reopening Hormuz in exchange for relief from sanctions and the naval blockade, while Washington continues to demand restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program. Previous ceasefire arrangements have failed to hold. Any durable settlement will depend on verification, which brings the inspectors back to the center. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Nearly half a century after the hostage crisis, America’s military capabilities have changed beyond recognition. The strategic question has not. Military success can be measured in destroyed targets. A durable political settlement requires a different accounting. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Cold War generation sustained a long and costly struggle because presidents explained the stakes in plain terms. Trump owes Americans the same plain talk now. He must tell them what victory in Iran looks like, and why it is worth $4+ gasoline. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ROBERT MAGINNIS

articles.title: Photos: Yemen’s hospitals struggle to operate amid persistent power outages
articles.summary: Families in Aden endure sleepless nights and spoiled food as blackouts become a defining feature of daily life.
articles.body:
Aden, Yemen – In this coastal city long accustomed to sweltering, humid summers, the absence of electricity can reshape an entire day.

When the power cuts out, fans and air conditioners fall silent. Sleep becomes difficult. Students race to finish their homework before darkness arrives. Children spill onto the streets while young men drift towards the sea in search of moving air and cooler waters.

Inside hospitals, where treatment cannot be postponed until the lights come back on, electricity carries a different weight altogether.

Yemen’s power crisis predates the current war. Even before the conflict, only about 55 percent of the population had access to electricity from all sources, which is among the lowest rates in the Middle East and North Africa.

Since 2015, damage to infrastructure, fuel shortages and ageing generation and distribution systems have left supplies even more fragile.

In Aden, power stations continue to face repeated shutdowns, leaving residents without electricity for long periods. Insurance premium increases on tankers carrying fuel to Aden have also reportedly made the crisis worse.

An assessment by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published this year said Aden was receiving just two to six hours of electricity a day as structural weaknesses and fuel shortages caused frequent outages.

As the sun sets over the city, a second part of the day begins. Homes and businesses slip into darkness, punctuated only by small lights powered by batteries and solar systems. Residents often do not know how long the latest blackout will last, or how long the power will stay on once it comes back.

During the summer, when temperatures in Aden climb towards 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), the consequences are hard to escape. Residents in the city interviewed in the middle of the year said their homes had become almost unbearable during the prolonged power cuts that plague the city. The heat does not always disappear when the sun goes down.

“Sometimes the power comes back while we are asleep, so we wake up to use it. Our lives have become tied to when electricity comes and goes,” one resident said. For her family, an outage is measured not just in hours but in problems. Children are unable to sleep, food spoils in warm refrigerators and housework must wait.

When the heat inside becomes too much, Youssef heads for the coast. The sea, he said, is no longer just a place of recreation but a refuge from the unbearable heat of the city.

“When the electricity is off for hours, it is very difficult to stay inside,” he said. “There is no fan and no air conditioning, and the humidity makes the heat worse, so we come to the sea.”

Towards the end of the day, young men and families gather along the waterfront. Some swim. Others simply sit beside the water and wait for the city to cool. But the sea cannot solve Aden’s electricity crisis. Hours later, Youssef returns home and sometimes finds the house exactly as he left it.

“Sometimes we get back and the power is still out, and we start waiting all over again,” he said.

For children like Mohammed, Saeed and Abdullah, blackouts have changed where childhood takes place. When their homes become too hot, they move into the street, running between houses or sitting with other children until late.

“It gets hot inside the house, so we come down and play in the street,” one of the boys said. “We play football or sit with our friends. Outside is better when the electricity is off.”

For them, a blackout is not an extraordinary event. It is part of the life they have grown up with.

The effects follow them into the classroom. In Aden, the United Nations Development Programme documented more than 7,000 students and teachers struggling in dark, stifling classrooms during power cuts. The installation of solar systems at eight schools and an education office has helped. One teacher reported that some students had fainted due to the heat.

At home, preparing for exams can depend on a rechargeable lamp or a small solar system if they have one.

In hospitals, there is no option but to simply wait out the darkness. Operating theatres, intensive care units, laboratories, medical refrigerators and dialysis machines all depend on continuous power.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says recurring power cuts disrupt lifesaving health services across Yemen, forcing facilities to rely on combinations of grid electricity, generators and solar systems.

In 2025, the WHO supplied about 4.33 million litres (1.14 million gallons) of fuel to 177 health facilities across the country to keep generators and essential equipment running.

Zeina Ahmed, a kidney patient, watches tubes carry her blood to a dialysis machine.

“For people at home, a power cut means heat and darkness. For us here, the first thing we think about is whether we will be able to have our dialysis or not,” she said.

“I come to the hospital knowing that I need this session. If it is delayed, I keep thinking about when I will get it and whether the machines will continue to work.”

After years of unreliable grid supply, solar panels, batteries and generators have become familiar parts of Yemen’s landscape.

They sit on rooftops, providing power to the homes, businesses and schools that can afford them.

More than half of Yemen’s homes now rely on solar power in some form, according to the WHO, while hospitals and other health facilities are increasingly adopting solar systems to keep essential services running.

Families who can afford to buy larger panels and batteries can power more appliances. Others might have just enough electricity for a light, a fan or a phone charger – a fragile shield against the dark and the heat.

articles.title: Anuv Jain: Rising Indian singer on new music and future hopes
articles.summary: The star reveals why he is "very selective" about releasing music - and shares his future collab hopes.
articles.body:
Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?

Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful".

The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene.

BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best".

"It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse.

Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager.

His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak.

Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing.

Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives and is personal to them.

His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple.

When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song.

"I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says.

"For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this."

Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists.

He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry.

Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space".

"We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says.

Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success.

Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently.

But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon".

"They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says.

"It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out."

The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out.

"There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet.

"When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it."

Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages of Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram.

There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years.

Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way".

"The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says.

However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart.

"He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain.

"Maybe the universe will just make it happen."

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv during German chancellor’s visit in a new escalation
articles.summary: Germany’s leader faced a grim new reality as his train pulled into Kyiv: air raid sirens and the boom of Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital.
articles.body: Germany’s leader faced a grim new reality as his train pulled into Kyiv: air raid sirens and the boom of Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital. During previous visits by international dignitaries of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s stature, the Kremlin paused or dramatically reduced attacks on the city. On Sunday, the sounds of war rang out repeatedly as the German delegation made its way around Kyiv, in what looks to be a new level of escalation by Moscow. On Monday, Germany’s foreign intelligence chief warned his country was at risk of becoming embroiled in a “violent conflict with Russia,” as Moscow steps up its “shadow war” against European democracies. Germany has been one of the most ardent supporters of Ukraine since the early days of the Russian invasion, supplying both military and financial aid. The country has also taken in more than a million Ukrainian refugees fleeing the war. Merz’s visit came as Russia has ramped up its around-the-clock strikes on Kyiv in recent weeks. The attacks and the air raid alerts that accompany them have severely disrupted life in the city, forcing millions to constantly seek shelter and paralyzing the capital’s businesses and transport networks. Over the last four days, including on the day Merz was visiting, Russia has hit several of Kyiv’s key bridges, with some strikes coming in broad daylight and as traffic was flowing through them — in what appears to be a new tactic to disrupt links between the capital’s two sides separated by the Dnipro River to further disable movement around Ukraine’s largest city. An air raid alert went off as Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited the site of a drone attack on the National Academy of Sciences last week. The dramatic daytime strike on the national landmark saw people clinging to windows to escape flames and thick smoke billowing out of the structure. Zelenskyy had to rush Merz off the site, calling it a “dangerous situation,” his office said in a statement. Merz reaffirmed Germany’s commitment to Ukraine over the weekend, and announced a further $1.1 billion in military aid. Germany, he said, would not be intimidated into abandoning Ukraine because it’s a “matter of Europe’s security” amid an escalating campaign of Russian hybrid warfare on the continent. The Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday it has been launching “massive strikes” against Kyiv in response to Ukraine’s threats to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry said Sunday it has disabled more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity in a string of successful strikes since this summer that have precipitated a major fuel crisis. In a separate statement, The Russian Defense Ministry said one of Kyiv’s bridges that came under attack Sunday was hit because it’s used to move troops and military cargo. Earlier, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals, including personnel of diplomatic missions, to leave the capital, saying Russian forces “will continue to carry out large-scale retaliatory strikes.” A similarly-worded warning was issued in May when Moscow also called for foreign diplomats to leave Kyiv, threatening an escalation. “We note with concern that not everyone has taken these warnings into account and that some individuals are knowingly placing themselves in mortal danger,” the ministry said. But like in May, Ukraine’s European allies are refusing to heed the Kremlin’s call to abandon the city. “Russia has a message for foreign diplomats in Kyiv: leave, or risk your lives,” Ambassador of the European Union Katarina Mathernova wrote on X. “Our answer: We are staying.”

articles.title: No 10 says RAF Fairford is 'safe' after US withdraws bombers
articles.summary: US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week.
articles.body:
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.

The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

A No 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

Peace for villagers as US bombers leave UK airbase

What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites?

He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".

Speaking on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.

He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."

Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident.

RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.

The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats."

It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year .

But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe.

Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks.

Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday.

articles.title: Students continue to protest in France as hundreds of schools close
articles.summary: Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday about 500 schools likely to be fully or partially closed on Monday.
articles.body:
Hundreds of high schools in France are closed as student protests continue against rundown schools and teacher shortages.

Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.

Earlier, National Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday evening, of the 3,700 schools, 400 to 500 were likely to be closed fully or partially on Monday.

Geffray said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked, while 78 teaching staff had been injured since the beginning of the protests.

Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.

Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences.

“We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said.

“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.

French news channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, northern France, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest and of a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.

Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school.

While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.

Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured.

French newspaper La Voix du Nord reported on Monday that a teenager lost a hand after picking up a police stun grenade.

Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while estimated costs of property damage are in the tens of millions of euros.

Student unions have called for a national day of demonstration on Tuesday.

articles.title: In Russia-occupied Oleshky, Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines
articles.summary: Ukrainians are turning to weeds for sustenance in a town where bodies are reportedly eaten by feral dogs.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – On the day of her 41st wedding anniversary, Vera Gulyaeva recalled her husband’s life and death.

In March, a Russian drone plunged into a bread line in the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky, killing several people and wounding Serhiy Gulyaev, a retired 63-year-old driver.

The town in the Kherson region had already been occupied for more than four years, and its 2,000 remaining residents spent the last two and a half years without electricity, running water, natural gas or healthcare.

The Gulyaevs, who had met at a friends’ wedding in 1985, lived in a small house they had built. They were reluctant to leave even after their children fled to Kyiv-controlled areas.

They had an orchid, a vegetable patch, five hens, a water well and a power generator that ran on the overpriced gas they occasionally bought from middlemen.

“I almost never left the house,” Gulyaeva, a stately 64-year-old retired schoolteacher told Al Jazeera. “The husband occasionally went out to buy bread.”

The bread-line attack left him with deep cranial wounds. She tried to get him to a hospital 80km (50 miles) away in the city of Skadovsk but failed as the ambulance ran over a landmine on the road.

Days later, a second attempt worked – but Gulyaev died in the hospital.

She recovered his remains, had them cremated and returned home with his ashes.

Now, she lives in western Ukraine with her daughter-in-law and two grandchildren while her son fights Russian forces.

Gulyaeva left behind all her family photos, friends and neighbours – several of whom have since died.

“People ate all of the food they’d stashed. People are starving,” Gulyaeva said of the food shortage stalking the town.

After four decades of teaching in the elementary school she had attended as a child, she still cannot fathom “how people can kill other people”.

Some residents survive on what they have farmed, stashed or found in abandoned apartments or houses. Others try to reach the nearest functioning grocery shop in the neighbouring village of Radensk, 20km (12.4 miles) away, to buy food.

A resident who fled the town but remains in contact with some residents told Al Jazeera that people have been killed by Russian drones or landmines. The bodies left out in the open are eaten by feral dogs.

On Thursday alone, there were four casualties. As they tried to get to Radensk, two people were killed and two were injured and brought back on a wheelbarrow and a bike.

“The choice that Russia leaves every day to civilian residents – stay and starve to death, leave and risk getting blown on a landmine,” Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram on Saturday.

European officials said the situation in Oleshky proves that Kyiv should not give in to Moscow’s demands to cede its land.

“When someone says: ‘Why don’t they just give up these territories?’ it sounds so simple. Right? But in reality, this is about the people who will suffer on those territories,” European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said on September 28.

Moscow, which has denied targeting civilians throughout the war, has acknowledged the humanitarian disaster but blamed Kyiv.

“There are, indeed, problems with delivering food and medical drugs [because] the Kyiv regime literally does everything to thwart these deliveries,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed on September 20. “Drones always hover in the air, killing people.”

Pro-Russian figures in occupied areas support his claims.

“Those who wanted to leave have left. No one is being held here,” an anonymous pro-Russian woman who runs a Telegram channel on life in Oleshky wrote on September 28. “Unfortunately, locals are afraid to speak on camera” because they have relatives on the Ukrainian side, she claimed. “The elderly live under Ukrainian shelling but are afraid to talk.”

Her claims are a far cry from what Ukrainian officials say.

Most Oleshky residents eat once a day, according to Tetiana Khasanenko, Oleshky’s mayor, who fled to the Kyiv-controlled side but maintains constant contact with the remaining residents.

Some have found old, dried macaroni to sustain themselves. Some eat whatever they manage to grow next to their houses. And some resort to common purslane – a watery weed that contains next to no protein and can be eaten raw.

“There’s no flour, no meat, no oil, no sugar, no salt,” Hasanenko told Al Jazeera. “There’s nothing.”

She accused Russia of using the residents as human shields.

Russian soldiers are a constant threat in the town with no functioning civilian administration, she said.

They move into the remaining houses without permission and force the residents to feed them and find alcohol.

“They’re often on drugs,” Hasanenko claimed. “But they’re armed. They threaten.”

Oleshky is about 10km (6 miles) west of the regional capital, Kherson, but Russians blew up the 1,400-metre (1,530-yard) bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Europe’s largest, in November 2022 while retreating from the city.

The delivery of food and drugs is perilous and complicated.

The last attempts to get lifesaving cargo to Oleshky in cars were cut short by landmines and drone attacks.

Ukraine has managed to fly several tonnes of food on drones, but retrieving it is complicated.

Most survivors have left their war-damaged houses and apartment buildings to move to the buildings that are more or less intact.

And even if some people manage to charge their mobile phones and contact the Ukrainian side, they “don’t give exact geolocations because they’re afraid”, Hasanenko said.

“Because if there’s a food drop, Russian soldiers will punish them for it,” she said.

Knowing about the remaining residents’ daily ordeal, those who escaped are tormented with guilt.

“You don’t get any joy from life knowing that something like that is happening in our country,” Gulyeva said. “This is a huge tragedy.”

articles.title: Arizona State cheerleader charged after confrontation with police caught on viral video
articles.summary: Viral police video shows Tempe, Arizona, officers throwing an Arizona State University cheerleader to the ground, leaving bruises on her face.
articles.body: Newly released police video shows officers throwing an Arizona State University cheerleader to the ground after she allegedly interfered with an ongoing arrest in Tempe, Arizona. ASU senior Eryn Bonner suffered bruises to her face after the July 19 incident, video of which shows one of the officers shove her to the ground and then pin her to a police bicycle before arresting her on the sidewalk. Bonner could be heard screaming, "Let him go! Let him go!" as police arrested two men who had been accompanying her. Bonner was charged last week with misdemeanor counts of disorderly conduct and hindering or interfering with police. Maricopa County prosecutors declined to move forward with felony charges against her. "Expecting public servants to live up to the highest standards of their profession is not an act of animosity toward those who serve with honor." We respectfully ask for your prayers and support as our daughter and our family continue to heal," the statement added. Surveillance footage from a nearby business captured the lead-up to the encounter, which shows Bonner and two male friends walk past a third man who had been standing on the sidewalk. articles.body: LUCKNOW: BSP national president Mayawati on Monday took her nephew Akash Anand back into the party and reappointed him as its national coordinator, three days after he apologised to her and expressed his willingness to serve the party under her leadership.In a post on X, Mayawati said that after “much deliberation”, the BSP had decided to give Anand another opportunity to work in the party as its national coordinator in the interest of the party and the movement.Mayawati said Anand’s “personality has largely been appropriate” within the party, but there had been reasons in recent days that required changes in the organisation.She said she hoped that after the retirement of Anand’s father-in-law, Ashok Siddharth, from politics, the party would function smoothly and there would be no need for repeated organisational changes.Anand was removed from the BSP on September 10, shortly after Siddharth announced his retirement from politics.Mayawati had said Anand’s failure to repost her appeal asking Siddharth to retire showed his attachment to family ties over the party and its movement. She had also said Anand needed greater political maturity.Three days ago, Anand apologised to Mayawati, saying his silence on her September 9 post had been misunderstood.He said he had distanced himself from social media at the time and sought forgiveness if his silence had hurt her.Anand also said the BSP was his family and that he wanted an opportunity to serve the party and its mission again under Mayawati’s leadership.Mayawati said on Monday that Anand’s request to return to the party had been accepted and that members of the family, including his father and younger brother Ishaan Anand, had also expressed their consent.The BSP chief also said that maintaining discipline in the party had been a priority and that members of her own family had not been exempt from strict decisions taken in the past.Anand’s return marks another reversal in his political relationship with Mayawati.He had earlier been expelled from the BSP in May 2024 and March 2025, and was taken back within a month on both occasions.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: Nigeria NYSC abductions: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Imo police say
articles.summary: The father of one of the 19 young abductees tells the BBC he hasn't eaten in three days out of worry.
articles.body:
Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives.

Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state.

The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping.

Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; £28,440), which he could not afford.

"There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.

Adewale appealed to the government for help.

Those kidnapped had been travelling from Ibadan in the south-west to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states on Thursday when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state.

The NYSC is a compulsory one-year programme for most Nigerian university and polytechnic graduates. Participants, known as corps members, are posted to different parts of the country to work and take part in community service, as well as to foster a sense of national unity.

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis

Speaking to journalists, Bosso said they had tracked the kidnappers.

"The drone actually showed us exactly their location. But our predicament is that with the intel we have... the camp is mined with IEDs [homemade bombs]," he said.

Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are being deployed as police prepare for a rescue operation.

Kidnapping for ransom is a major security problem in Nigeria, involving both criminal gangs and armed groups.

The abduction in Imo state has caused widespread concern, with mass kidnappings less common in southern Nigeria than in some parts of the north.

Paying ransoms is illegal and authorities have repeatedly warned families against doing so, but relatives of kidnapped people are often under pressure to do so to secure their release.

The latest abduction highlights the risks faced by young people travelling across Nigeria to do their national youth service and has renewed calls for reforms.

The NYSC has previously said it would not deploy members to areas considered high-risk because of violence or the threat of abduction. Most parts of south-eastern Nigeria have not previously been classified as high-risk areas.

In the south-east, some previous abductions have been linked to separatist groups, including the Indigenous People of Biafra (Ipob).

Authorities have not linked the current abduction to any group.

articles.title: Man jailed for life over failed knife attack at Israeli embassy in London
articles.summary: Abdullah Albadri arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days before trying to break into the embassy with two knives.
articles.body:
A failed asylum seeker who tried to break into the Israeli embassy in London to carry out a knife attack has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 20 years.

Abdullah Albadri was carrying two knives when police officers caught him as he tried to climb over a fence into the Kensington embassy on 28 April 2025.

The 34-year-old from Kuwait had arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days earlier, having first entered country illegally four years earlier.

He was previously found guilty by majority verdict after a trial at the Old Bailey of preparation of terrorist acts and possession of two bladed articles.

The court heard how he was motivated to plot the attack by the death of Palestinians in Gaza and planned the attack after sleeping rough in the capital.

Albadri first travelled to the UK on a small boat in August 2021 and applied for asylum but returned to France before a decision was made.

He crossed the Channel again in April 2025 and was housed in a hotel in Basingstoke for three days, before being told he was not eligible for accommodation due to his outstanding asylum application.

On the day of the attempted attack, he walked to the west London embassy from north London wearing a red and white traditional Arabic scarf wrapped around his head and sunglasses.

The embassy is located on a street which is home to several large diplomatic buildings and has a round-the-clock police presence.

At around 18:00, he saluted in the direction of two nearby diplomatic protection officers before trying to scale a security fence.

The armed officers dragged him down from the railings and detained him.

When he was searched, police found two 10cm (4ins)-long blades and a handwritten copy of a verse titled "the benefit of martyrdom".

His trial heard how he told police: "I want to make a crime inside there. Why are you stopping me? Why are you stopping me from making crimes?"

During a later interview at a police station, he said he had wanted "to do something to stop the war".

The Old Bailey also heard evidence he may have acted in a way to force the nearby armed officers to kill him.

Prosecutor Catherine Pattison said Albadri "intended to do something that would have resulted in the sacrifice of his life".

She told the court people were leaving the embassy when he attempted to scale the fence who "would not have had any chance to defend themselves" if he had been able to carry out the attack.

Defence barrister Chris Henley said Albadri's plan "could never ever have succeeded", adding "there was no serious risk of any harm to anybody".

He said Albadri had acted in an "absurd, performative fashion" which was "deliberately designed to draw attention to himself".

Albadri had spent the morning "trying to get help" to access housing, his defence barrister told the court.

His trial previously heard he told officers "I wish you'd use that on me", and replied "I might be yeah" when asked if he was referring to a rifle.

On Monday, Mrs Justice Lambert KC sentenced Albadri to life in prison with a minimum term of 20 years.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London, said: "Albadri's attempt to carry out a terrorist attack at the embassy was thwarted due to the courageous and swift actions of officers on duty, who prevented him from breaching the security perimeter.

"The significant prison sentence he has received reflects the danger he posed on the day and the lack of remorse he has shown since he was arrested."

She said the Israeli embassy had "face various security alerts in recent times" and security measures were in place to "ensure the site and the wider community is kept as safe as possible".

articles.title: Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism?
articles.summary: Israel condemns the move as the party’s vote causes an uproar, including among party members.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom’s Green Party has voted to define Zionism as a form of racism, drawing condemnation from the Israeli government.

In a binding vote held at the party’s conference over the weekend, members voted to usher in the new definition as well as a series of other strongly pro-Palestine policies.

However, just as the resolution has drawn international criticism, it has also proved internally controversial with four of the party’s five members in parliament opposing it.

Israel on Monday banned party leader Zack Polanski from the country just a day before the politician faces a by-election as he runs in the London constituency that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer represented.

Zionism emerged as a political ideology in the late 19th century. It called for the creation of a Jewish homeland at a time of rising anti-Semitism and persecution of Jews in Europe. Theodore Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist considered the father of political Zionism, originally proposed an independent and colonial Jewish state in either Palestine or Argentina.

Here’s what we know about what the Greens have said:

The Greens endorsed the motion to equate Zionism with racism by a vote of 1,022 to 813.

In addition, the party restated its “commitment to Palestinian liberation” and called for the “establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”.

The party also recommitted to its support of Palestinians’ right of return as well as to the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement against Israel.

“The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians,” a Green Party statement said.

A significant number of party members, including four of its five MPs, were against parts of the resolution, exposing divisions within the party.

Codeputy leader Rachel Millward said in a post on X that while the party is committed to “stop the genocide”, the term Zionism means “different things to different people, … so I personally do not think the policy helps us do the work we all want to”.

Meanwhile, Polanski, who is Jewish and was away campaigning during the vote, told journalists afterwards that if Zionism equates to the displacement of Palestinians, “that is clearly racist.”

Polanski said he, however, did not support the reference to a single Palestinian state and external entities should not decide what a future state would look like.

Israel has accused the party of legitimising “terrorism”, and senior officials equated it to anti-Semitism.

“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on social media.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would “deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the party was “racist”.

The Green Party has rejected equating criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism and reiterated its stance against “any form of discrimination or harassment”.

“We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people,” Polanski and other senior party members said in a statement on Sunday.

Has Zionism been equated to racism before?

Yes. In 1975, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution that “determines that Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”.

The vote was sponsored by the Soviet bloc and the Arab League. It passed after 72 countries, largely from the Middle East and Africa, voted for it. Israel and 34 other countries – chiefly from the West – were against it. Thirty-two other countries abstained.

Just a year before, at the 1974 General Assembly, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat had given his “olive branch” speech at the General Assembly.

About the same time, African countries opposing the apartheid regime in South Africa, which was increasingly allying with Israel, had resolved separately that the Israeli government was “racist” and both had an “imperialist origin.”

Also, in 1975, at the first international women’s conference, held in Mexico City, attendees decided there would be no international peace outside the “elimination of foreign occupation, Zionism, apartheid” and all other forms of “racial discrimination”.

However, the General Assembly vote proved controversial. Chaim Herzog, then-Israeli ambassador to the UN and later president, told the assembly in a speech that it was “based on hatred, falsehood and arrogance” and proceeded to rip up copies of the resolution in front of the audience.

The US too accused the UN of making “anti-Semitism international law”.

In December 1991, the US, under President George HW Bush, stepped up a campaign to revoke the resolution with Bush declaring at the UN that equating Zionism with racism “is to reject Israel itself” and to “challenge its right to exist”.

Israel also insisted it would not participate in the Madrid Peace Process to continue negotiations between Israel and Palestinian leaders if the resolution was not cancelled.

After much pressure from the US, an overwhelming majority of countries voted for its revocation – 111 to 25, including European and African countries.

Jewish Voice for Peace, the American anti-Zionist and pro-Palestinian advocacy group, has also named Zionism as a movement that creates a “racist hierarchy with European Jews at the top”.

In a February statement, the group reiterated its stance against what it called the “colonial ideology” of Zionism’s founders.

Similarly, in the United Kingdom, an employment tribunal in 2024 backed anti-Zionist activist and professor David Miller, who was earlier sacked from his post at the University of Bristol in 2021 for his views that the movement was “inherently racist”.

articles.title: A squadron inside one jet:  US, China are racing to build 6th-gen fighters, redefine air warfare
articles.summary: As tensions simmer in the Indo-Pacific, the US and China are developing a new, more powerful generation of fighter aircraft for a potential conflict.
articles.body: As tensions simmer in the Indo-Pacific, the US and China are developing a new, more powerful generation of fighter aircraft for a potential conflict. Unlike earlier fighters that relied heavily on speed and manoeuvrability, these aircraft will use stealth, artificial intelligence and connectivity as key advantages.Even as fifth-generation fighters such as the F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II and China's J-20 have transformed stealth, sensor fusion and situational awareness, military planners are already preparing for the next era of aerial combat. Sixth-generation fighters are being designed not simply as advanced aircraft, but as command nodes within a highly connected battlefield ecosystem incorporating unmanned systems and multidomain strike capabilities.Those in the race for sixth-generation dominanceChina and the United States are currently at the forefront of the sixth-generation race, followed by the United Kingdom, Japan, Italy and several other European nations.Programmes such as the US Air Force's Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD), the US Navy's F/A-XX, the UK-Japan-Italy Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), and the French-led Future Combat Air System (FCAS) all aim to field operational aircraft in the 2030s.China, meanwhile, has shown considerable momentum with the testing of advanced prototypes identified as the J-36 and J-50. Unlike previous generations, which focused primarily on speed, manoeuvrability and stealth, sixth-generation programmes aim to redefine air combat by integrating manned and unmanned systems, advanced AI and capabilities designed to operate in heavily contested environments.The need for a new generation of fightersThe push towards sixth-generation aircraft is being driven as much by geopolitical changes as by technological advances. Since the end of the Cold War, the United States has enjoyed largely unchallenged dominance in military aviation. But China's rapid air force modernisation, increasingly sophisticated Russian air defences and the growing complexity of future battlefields have raised questions about how long existing aircraft can remain effective.A key driver is the rise of anti-access/area-denial environments. Countries such as China have invested heavily in integrated air-defence networks, long-range missiles, electronic warfare and anti-satellite capabilities designed to prevent adversaries from operating freely in contested regions.In a potential conflict over Taiwan or elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, aircraft may have to operate far from friendly bases, making range and endurance critical. At the same time, advances in radar, passive sensors and AI could erode the stealth advantage enjoyed by fifth-generation fighters. Future aircraft will therefore need to reduce not only their radar cross-section but also their thermal and electromagnetic signatures.What makes a sixth-generation fighter?Although there is no universally agreed definition, several characteristics are emerging as hallmarks of sixth-generation fighters.Artificial intelligence is expected to form the backbone of future combat aviation, functioning less as a replacement for pilots and more as a digital co-pilot capable of processing vast amounts of information in real time. AI systems could assist with threat analysis, navigation, sensor management, electronic warfare and target prioritisation.No pilot can realistically process all the information generated during modern air combat. AI could filter that data and recommend courses of action, allowing pilots to focus on mission objectives while humans retain final control over lethal decisions.Closely linked to this is manned-unmanned teaming, one of the biggest shifts in sixth-generation combat. Future fighters are expected to operate alongside autonomous or semi-autonomous drones, often described as loyal wingmen or Collaborative Combat Aircraft.These drones could perform reconnaissance, electronic warfare, strike, decoy or communications-relay missions, allowing commanders to send less expensive and potentially expendable platforms into the most dangerous environments. A single pilot could eventually direct several drones, multiplying the combat power of one aircraft.Survivability is also becoming more important. Fifth-generation stealth has largely focused on reducing radar cross-section, particularly from the front. Sixth-generation designs aim to reduce detectability across multiple domains and from a wider range of angles, including infrared signatures from engines and electromagnetic emissions that could reveal an aircraft's position.Advanced electronic warfare systems will also be used to confuse or deceive enemy sensors. In an increasingly networked battlespace, survivability will depend as much on information superiority and situational awareness as on avoiding detection.Information and connectivity key to victoryPerhaps the biggest shift is the move from platform-centric to network-centric warfare. Future fighters are expected to operate within a shared combat cloud linking aircraft, drones, satellites, ships, ground forces and command centres.Data gathered by one platform could be shared across the network, allowing every connected system to act on a common picture of the battlefield. In this model, the fighter becomes less important as an individual platform and more important as a node within a much larger combat network.Many countries are also developing adaptive-cycle engines capable of dynamically adjusting performance. They can switch between high-performance output and greater fuel efficiency depending on mission requirements. Unlike conventional engines, which typically prioritise either efficiency or power, adaptive-cycle designs aim to deliver both while improving range and thermal management.Directed-energy weapons, including high-energy lasers, are also under development. Power generation and thermal management remain major challenges, but continued research could eventually make such weapons practical for defending against missiles, drones and sensors.The sixth-generation fighter is no longer a futuristic concept; it is the current gold standard because it redefines air combat as a networked, AI-enabled system of systems, rather than just a faster, stealthier airframe. For the IAF, looking at sixth-generation technology now is not about chasing technology; it is about ensuring that when our next-generation fighters enter service, they are built around the right combat architecture — manned-unmanned teaming, combat-cloud networking and adaptive sensing — so that we do not spend the next 30-odd years trying to retrofit legacy platforms for a war they were never designed to fight.US seeks to retain its leadThe United States aims to maintain its long-standing lead through the Next Generation Air Dominance programme, conceived as a family of systems rather than a single aircraft and built around the Boeing-developed F-47.The aircraft is expected to combine extended range, advanced stealth and close integration with collaborative drones, with a particular focus on long-range operations across the Indo-Pacific.The US Navy is pursuing the parallel F/A-XX programme to replace parts of its Super Hornet fleet with a similarly networked and drone-enabled capability.The US has already begun testing Collaborative Combat Aircraft at scale, including Boeing's MQ-28 during Exercise Valiant Shield in 2026 in the Western Pacific.China's rapid progressionChina's progress has drawn close scrutiny. The successful fielding of the J-20 demonstrated Beijing's ability to challenge traditional Western leadership in advanced fighter design. More recent sightings of the J-36 and J-50 suggest China could be moving rapidly towards sixth-generation capability.Both aircraft appear to feature advanced stealth shaping, tailless configurations and design concepts consistent with networked warfare. The programmes also fit China's broader military modernisation strategy and its emphasis on system-of-systems warfare, a concept that closely mirrors Western visions of future combat.If current trends continue, China could become the first serious competitor capable of challenging the United States across multiple dimensions of advanced military aviation.Europe advances on the drawing boardEurope's approach has centred on multinational collaboration rather than independent national programmes.GCAP brings together the United Kingdom, Japan and Italy to develop an advanced multirole aircraft expected to enter service around 2035. The aircraft is intended to replace the Eurofighter Typhoon and Japan's F-2 while preserving long-term industrial independence.Meanwhile, FCAS, originally a joint programme between France, Germany and Spain, continues under French leadership following Germany's exit. It is built around a New Generation Fighter, remote-carrier drones and a shared digital combat cloud.Together, these programmes reflect Europe's effort to maintain strategic autonomy rather than rely heavily on American aircraft.India joins the raceIndia has also entered the sixth-generation conversation. Defence minister Rajnath Singh has said India intends to develop not only a fifth-generation but also a sixth-generation fighter.The statement comes as the Indian Air Force's squadron strength stands at 29 against a sanctioned strength of 42, roughly 70% of its authorised level.The defence ministry has confirmed that India is engaging with both GCAP and FCAS. France now leads FCAS, with Spain remaining a partner. FCAS is expected to make its first flight around 2028-29, broadly aligning with the planned first flight of India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft.The split between France and Germany could, in some respects, work in India's favour. Disagreements over carrier operability and nuclear delivery capabilities contributed to Germany's exit, while India already possesses both capabilities, bringing its operational requirements closer to those of France.For India, engagement with both programmes appears aimed less at choosing a single partner and more at securing a role in shaping the next generation of aerial combat.As traditional close-range aerial combat becomes less central to modern air warfare, information dominance, electronic warfare and long-range engagement could emerge as decisive factors. Pilots may increasingly function as mission commanders directing groups of drones rather than personally engaging individual targets.As warfare becomes more integrated across the air, land, sea, space and cyber domains, victory may ultimately depend less on individual platforms and more on the effectiveness of the broader combat ecosystem.

articles.body: Welcome to Screencaps, "America's Best Daily Column," as named by the readers.
