articles.title: Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz?
articles.summary: Crude exports bypassing Hormuz surged in September, yet oil prices remain high. Could a secret fee be the reason?
articles.body:
Middle East oil exports have climbed back above levels seen before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, despite Tehran’s attempts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and attack vessels.

Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September, reaching between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day (bpd), according to provisional data from maritime tracking firm Kpler. Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd.

This surge in oil exports from the region has so far largely been attributed to US ships shepherding tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with increasing ship-to-ship transfers that reduce the risks of being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones. Meanwhile, the fact that oil prices have remained high has been explained by analysts as the result of still-elevated insurance rates — driven by fears of Iranian attacks — and a market factoring in the possibility of a return to a hot war.

But a senior Kpler analyst last week offered a different explanation for the rise in oil exports at high prices. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo.

Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

Does this explanation hold up, and what does it mean for the war and oil prices?

Michelle Brohard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, recently said some countries could be paying Iran for passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

“I suspect there is a toll that’s being paid, which is giving these ships safe passage,” she said in an interview last week with energy analyst Rory Johnston.

“I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added.

“So you’re starting to see like what I would call like a race to get out as much as possible, as quickly as possible before the war restarts.”

The claim has not been independently verified, and Brohard presented it as speculation rather than a finding backed by evidence.

But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait.

The Trump administration, during the course of the war, has repeatedly said Iran will not be permitted to charge a toll under any potential agreement with Washington.

Closure of the strait has caused global fuel costs to soar and has tested agricultural sectors across the world.

What does traffic in the Hormuz look like?

Oil is increasingly getting out of the Middle East, marine trackers report.

In the last week of September, the seven-day average climbed above the roughly 18 million bpd recorded before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February – the first time since the conflict started.

Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September.

The pattern of increasing oil exports has continued into October. Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company on Saturday announced that it had transported two million barrels of crude on a very ‌large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general said was the company’s first such operation in decades.

According to Kpler, “40 percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore”, with much of it flowing through Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pipelines.

The export figures also include supplies moved through the Red Sea, which has become an increasingly important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Moreover, the Kpler figures exclude any vessels that may have crossed the key transit route with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.

Iran, however, disputes suggestions that it has lost control of the waterway.

Senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi said on Sunday only three to four million bpd were travelling along a US-supervised route and described that amount as “negligible” compared with pre-war traffic.

Before the war erupted seven months ago, the strait routinely saw about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships.

Oil prices have eased marginally as exports from the Middle East recover. Last week, the Group of Seven countries also announced a decision to release 100 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves.

But crude prices remain significantly higher than pre-war levels. Brent crude was trading at about $101.59 a barrel on Monday, down 0.71 percent, while US West Texas Intermediate fell 1.2 percent to about $90.05.

“Despite exports from the region resurging, much will depend, longer-term, on the security of energy supplies,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noting that the “situation is still tense”.

“The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with the attack on another tanker on Sunday keeping worries bubbling about the potential for further disruption to supplies, particularly if shipping companies become increasingly reluctant to risk sending vessels through the crucial chokepoint.”

On Monday, an oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was instructed by the IRGC to turn back or risk being targeted, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) group that monitors shipping traffic.

Does the Kpler analyst’s claim hold weight?

Academic Abdul Khalique says while Kpler analyst Brohard’s speculation that a transit-fee arrangement has been put in place may be “plausible”, it is best described as an “informal security mechanism rather than a formal maritime levy”.

“No public proof confirms a systematic, state-run Iranian toll system,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.

He said the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) safeguards transit passage through international straits, “rendering formal tolls legally dubious”.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that Brohard’s suspected scenario was “in part” possible.

“Everything appears to be happening under the radar in the Middle East, from the US convoying ships to Iran quietly charging tolls,” he told Al Jazeera.

In September, the US government also imposed sanctions on a digital assets firm, BitBank, that it said had been used by Iran’s Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority — a body set up by the country’s government to collect fees for allowing the safe transit of vessels through the strait — to transfer money to Tehran.

However, Beauchamp said the biggest challenge for oil exports was now what he called the “problem of shipping”.

“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships, and that has pushed freight rates higher while also reducing supply beyond the region itself,” he added.

According to Beauchamp, Asian buyers are having to find crude from further away too, “lengthening transit times”.

“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping. While less exciting, it is arguably much more important and trickier to solve,” he said.

articles.title: Glasgow City Council and Unison reach agreement in pay and grading row
articles.summary: The local authority says this means it will not consider dismissing and rehiring its staff.
articles.body:
Glasgow City Council and the largest council union, Unison, have reached an agreement in a pay and grading dispute.

The local authority says this means it will not consider firing and rehiring more than 23,000 staff.

The dispute was over the new pay and grading structure designed to deal with the underlying issues which led to thousands of equal pay claims from female workers past and present.

The original proposal would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of employees but, under the new deal, their salaries will now be protected for three years.

Unison said negotiations were continuing and it would ballot its members later this month.

Glasgow City Council pauses plan to fire and rehire 23,000 staff

Council leader Ricky Bell said: "I am delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison.

"This deal means we are able to remove the unpalatable prospect of fire and rehire, with proposals put to members in a ballot later this month."

Bell added that it was a "strong and fair deal" and confirmed that both the GMB and Unite unions had also agreed to take it to their members.

He said: "With all three unions now engaging with their memberships, we are moving closer to the outcome we have always wanted to achieve: ending pay discrimination in Glasgow City Council once and for all."

The council leader said additional support from the Scottish government had "helped unlock this agreement" and thanked the unions for their engagement.

He concluded: "While there is no further money to come as part of this package, I look forward to the outcome of the ballots in the coming weeks.

"We have always been clear that our goal is to deliver a fair, sustainable pay and grading system that works for employees and protects vital public services. We are now closer than ever to achieving that."

Unison said it had secured "major improvements on pay and grading".

It also confirmed that a proposal for pay protection for workers facing losses had been increased to three years.

The council has also agreed to continue discussions with the union on outstanding issues including lower-paid workers, allowances, unevaluated jobs, equality impacts and the operation of the new pay model.

Unison said the breakthrough created a route towards a ballot of its membership, without the council dictating the union's recommendation or communications.

The union added that important issues remained unresolved but negotiations would continue before members voted.

Chris Sermanni, Glasgow City Unison branch secretary, said: "Unison stood firm because Glasgow's workers deserved better than what was originally put on the table.

"That position has secured significant movement.

"There's now a path for Unison members to give their verdict without the immediate threat of dismissal and re-engagement hanging over them."

Sermanni stressed that the union had not accepted the pay and grading package and said the "fight for improvements" was not over.

"Thousands of workers are owed substantial and long-overdue increases and we want them to receive every penny," he said.

"At the same time, other workers face significant losses and some still don't even know their final outcome.

"The period ahead will be used to keep fighting to give the whole workforce the information they need to make their decision."

Mandy McDowall, Unison Scotland regional organiser, said the intervention of the Scottish government had "helped create the space for further progress".

The timetable for the ballot, which will last four weeks, will be confirmed soon.

articles.title: Medicine shortage eases as first tender supplies reach KMSCL warehouses
articles.summary: Kerala medicine shortage eases as first tender drug supplies reach KMSCL warehouses; full delivery due by Oct 15, with emergency закупки to cover gaps.
articles.body: T’puram: State’s medicine shortage has begun to ease, with the first consignments of drugs procured through fresh tenders reaching Kerala Medical Services Corporation Ltd (KMSCL) warehouses. The corporation said the remaining supplies are expected to arrive by Oct 15.Stocks of seven medicines, including drugs used to treat heart ailments and hypertension, have started reaching the warehouses. The first batches of antiobiotic doxycycline have arrived, while medicines for diabetes and filariasis have also been received. Supplies of Vitamin A medicine administered to children are expected to reach the warehouses on Monday, KMSCL officials said.Medicines including aspirin are also expected to arrive shortly. Officials said around 25% of the medicines covered under the latest tender orders would be supplied in the first phase, with the entire quantity expected to be delivered by Oct 15.Health minister K Muraleedharan said there was no severe shortage of medicines in govt hospitals and termed reports suggesting otherwise unfortunate. He said shortages of certain medicines were being addressed through emergency procurement.The minister said the supply disruption was partly caused by companies withdrawing from the market in the wake of the West Asia conflict. Medicines in short supply were being procured through ready-purchase arrangements to ensure uninterrupted treatment, he said.The minister also said companies found to have supplied poor-quality medicines had been excluded from procurement.Muraleedharan alleged that certain companies were behind reports highlighting the shortage in govt hospitals and accused them of attempting to project state’s public healthcare system in a negative light. “There may be shortcomings, but govt will not succumb to such a campaign,” he said. .Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news. articles.title: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall
articles.summary: The new director of news takes over from Deborah Turness, who resigned as CEO last year.
articles.body:
Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for the BBC's director of news. She is a well-regarded high flier who has impressed in her roles at Panorama, Newsnight and Channel 4 News.

She is currently the BBC's director of news documentaries and long form journalism. But she hasn't been in that role for long and hasn't spent years leading huge teams of people (BBC News' global newsroom has around 4,500 staff).

A lack of that kind of experience might have been problematic in the past. But the BBC's new director general comes from Google. Tech companies regularly appoint people who may not have the direct experience for a role but have the strategic vision and drive to make a difference. He is talking about distinctive journalism and reinvention.

Jupp's appointment signals a direction of travel both on the change that the new boss thinks is required and also on the use of technology.

Before Jupp took up her role in documentaries, she had moved to the US and was a senior member of the BBC's AI team, developing and leading the BBC's approach to artificial intelligence.

It feels significant that the former Google boss has chosen someone with that experience to run his news teams, raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom.

But the new director of news has a lot on her plate.

She leads a news operation that is still reeling from a series of crises that eventually brought down her predecessor, Deborah Turness, as well as director general Tim Davie.

She'll have to oversee the £51m in savings that news must make (one tenth of the £500m the entire BBC must find).

Job cuts are already in train, journalists are having to reapply for their roles - and there is much more pain to come.

Staff have told me they want clear direction and an end to the salami slicing of resources. They ask what are the priorities, what are the things we do that are crucial and which are less important?

The teams she now leads will want a plan for how they can make such deep cuts without impacting the quality of what they do.

BBC News stands or falls by its on-the-ground, eyewitness journalism. Some are asking how much of that can BBC News still afford to do.

But there are also questions about whether the BBC needs to learn from its rivals by slimming down the number of stories it does and prioritizing the big hits. A streamlined BBC News.

Her challenges are both editorial and practical.

After 10 months without a permanent boss, I have picked up a sense of drift. Everybody understands - and the new DG repeats this, just as his predecessor Tim David did - that the BBC must go to where audiences are and where they will be in the future.

Staff at BBC News have heard this before. They want to know what it actually means in practice and how news will be reorganised.

The biggest challenge is the change in viewing habits. News has a loyal base of viewers still watching on linear channels (and who many argue should not be taken for granted in the rush to attract younger audiences online) but the direction of travel is changing fast.

There will be resistance - from viewers, from politicians, from campaign groups - as the BBC decides to move away from old formats and old technology. But it must go where audiences are and the new head of news will need a strategy to move much more deeply into a digital world.

The BBC has been doing this in a fairly piecemeal way up to now.

But Jupp will need to turbocharge it - with fewer resources and a demoralised workforce, some of whom she will need to shepherd out the door.

Brittin has talked about the bigger prize of getting the news division's trusted journalism to much larger numbers of people around the world. She has to deliver that.

She will also need to give BBC News greater editorial confidence after years of political attack and the errors of recent years.

Staff working in news would argue it was the current affairs side of the operation that previously let the organisation down. A documentary about the children of Gaza narrated by the son of a Hamas official. A documentary about Israel's assault on Gazan medical staff commissioned and then dropped by the BBC and later shown on Channel 4.

Then, of course, there are the revelations that a Panorama broadcast ahead of Donald Trump's reelection as President had spliced together two clips of the President's speech on the day of the riots on Capitol Hill - changing the editorial meaning. BBC chair Samir Shah apologised to Trump who is suing the BBC for $10bn. The court proceedings are still playing out.

Perhaps promoting Jupp - who took over the BBC News' current affairs department after the scandals - to the top of News is a signal she will grip what some have viewed as a weak spot with rigour.

Trust is one of the BBC's core values. It's listed on the back of our work passes as "the foundation of the BBC". The new boss will need to make sure that the BBC remains the place of record. An organisation that is trusted.

It's still the most trusted source of news, but there are growing numbers of people on all sides of the political spectrum who don't feel the BBC speaks for them.

Many will argue that is because people live in echo chambers online, and don't want to hear other voices.

BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news

articles.title: US pulls bombers from UK base: Is Iran manoeuvring Trump’s war plans?
articles.summary: The withdrawal means the US lost a convenient launchpad, not its underlying strike capability, said an expert.
articles.body:
Last week, a British bomb disposal robot roamed the area near the Royal Air Force (RAF) base at Fairford and 85 homes were evacuated as the threat of an attack appeared imminent.

Days later, the United States speedily sent B-1 bombers stationed there, which were used to strike Iran in its ongoing war, back home. About a dozen had been stationed at the air base.

The foiled incident resulted in no charges and the release of five suspects , and subsequently a separate British-Iranian suspect. But the US cited concerns about more potential attacks for its decision to withdraw its fleet. Tehran has denied any link to the alleged plot to target the base.

RAF Fairford was a pit stop for US bombers during the war – but more importantly, it allowed Washington to rapidly unleash intensive strikes on Iran, say analysts.

They added that their withdrawal reduces Washington’s ability to rapidly generate and sustain bombing missions, but it will not prevent the US from continuing to strike Iran.

“The United States has lost a convenient launchpad, not its underlying strike capability,” Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum and a lecturer at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera.

Long bombing campaigns made more demanding

The analysts were in agreement that the British base gave the US a faster and more efficient way to sustain strikes on Iran.

The bombers at the Fairford base were officially stationed there for defensive strikes – at the behest of the UK government – and likely had a modest targeting list, said Christoph Bergs, an analyst at the world’s oldest defence and security thinktank, the Royal United Services Institute.

“Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat,” Bergs told Al Jazeera.

Thafer explained that while the loss of the bombers does not remove the US’s ability to strike or escalate, “depending on where other assets are positioned, it could make a prolonged bombing campaign more demanding”.

The removal of B-1 bombers imposes a number of tactical costs, says Arun Dawson. He is a PhD candidate at King’s College London’s Freeman Air and Space Institute and a researcher with the UK Nuclear Deterrence Network.

Unlike the more modern B-2 stealth bomber designed to make enemy tracking difficult – which has also previously been stationed at RAF Fairford – “the B-1’s principal advantage is its conventional weapons payload – the largest of any aircraft in the US military”, Dawson told Al Jazeera. The B-1 carries at least 34 tonnes of ordnance, he said.

“This makes the B-1 particularly effective at delivering large volumes of precision-guided weapons against multiple targets during a prolonged air campaign,” said Dawson.

“In the Iran war, those targets may include air-defence infrastructure, ballistic missile sites and IRGC facilities,” he added, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

With the B-1s withdrawing, the US may now have to rely more heavily on longer-range missions from the US or other distant bases, increasing flight times, crew fatigue and the need for aerial refuelling, he explained.

Still, the US may have made the withdrawal decision based on an examination of risks, said Dawson.

“Their abrupt departure suggests that specific threats may have been directed at the aircraft, their crews or the base itself,” he said.

Washington may have also calculated that temporarily withdrawing the bombers could protect it for future operations, especially if the US does not expect the Iran war to intensify any time soon, said Dawson.

For David Des Roches, a professor at the Thayer Marshall Institute and a former Pentagon official, the B-1 withdrawal suggests that the risks outweighed the benefits of keeping the jets at the UK airbase.

The security incident last week “exposed a vulnerability” as the aircraft were “out in the open” and only about 300 yards (275 metres) from where the public could see them.

“So they were very vulnerable to, say, drone attacks or other kind[s] of mortar attacks,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Just a small drone or any kind of a drone with explosives on board could conceivably cause significant damage,” said Des Roches.

The former Pentagon official acknowledged that the deployment of the US bombers means “you lose a little bit of operational ability,” but said that given the threat seen at Fairford, “we should have had overhead cover for all of our aircraft, globally, years ago”.

The US has two potential options if the bombers are to be redeployed: to Diego Garcia, the remote coral atoll in the central Indian Ocean hosting both a US and UK military base; or to its many US bases in the Gulf .

Thafer pointed out that Diego Garcia offers greater protection from potential Iranian attacks, but requires longer flight distances.

Rerouting the bombers to Diego Garcia will also depend on how quickly additional aircraft can be folded into the local basing infrastructure, pointed out Bergs.

Stationing them in the Gulf closer to Iran would give them the advantage of shortened transit times, reduced tanker requirements and the ability to generate sorties more rapidly, said Dawson.

But basing in the Gulf region, the analysts agreed, will require more deliberate negotiations around risk mitigation, given that these countries have taken the brunt of Iranian counterstrikes throughout the war. They also want to avoid being seen as direct participants in a US campaign against Iran.

Fairford had therefore offered a “useful” middle ground between the two options, said Thafer.

But with Fairford no longer an option, Diego Garcia would be the more obvious choice, Dawson said, offering not only greater distance from Iran but also a more secure operating environment. It has infrastructure designed to support large-scale US air operations, he said.

For now, the withdrawal appears to blunt rather than eliminate US bombing capacity against Iran.

However, the practical impact on US military options will depend largely on whether the administration sees a need for such strikes now, or whether the threat posed by similar aircraft stationed at Diego Garcia is sufficient for the time being, said Bergs.

The expected arrival of the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force to the Middle East by November, meanwhile, will add significant US carrier-based air power in the region, said Dawson.

“Aircraft for aircraft, carrier fighters cannot substitute for the B-1’s enormous payload, but there are many more of them, giving commanders additional options for shorter-range strikes,” he said.

What this episode highlights, said the researcher, is the importance – and the vulnerability – of the US’ alliances and overseas basing.

Washington has long enjoyed access to a global network of military facilities – which has been key for its ability to project power rapidly and at scale, he said.

But if those bases face attacks or political restrictions – the implications would extend beyond the Iran war, warned Dawson.

They would affect “how the US military structures its forces, distributes its assets, generates combat power and sustains operations overseas”.

articles.title: Pitripaksh footfall in Gaya crosses 32 lakh, highest in years
articles.summary: Pitripaksh Mela in Gaya sees record 32.94 lakh devotees by day 9, highest in years; officials tighten crowd management at Vishnupad Temple.
articles.body: Gaya: The footfall of devotees during the fortnight-long Pitripaksh Mela crossed 32.94 lakh by Sunday, the ninth day of the event in Gaya, making it the highest turnout in recent years and surpassing last year’s figure of around 30 lakh.The district administration released the turnout data based on readings from electronic foot-counting machines installed at Vishnupad Temple and other major pind vedis across the city.On Monday, the 10th day of the mela, district magistrate Shashank Shubhankar inspected Vishnupad Temple premises, including the sanctum sanctorum, exit gates, ghats, cremation ground area, Gayakup Vedi and the control room at Sanwas Sadan Samiti.During the inspection, an elderly woman devotee from Madhya Pradesh felt unwell near the temple exit amid heavy crowding. DM directed medical personnel to examine her and provide glucose and medicines if required.DM asked officials to closely monitor crowd movement inside the sanctum and at exit points through live CCTV feeds. He stressed the need to assist elderly, women and vulnerable devotees and ensure their safe movement after darshan.At the control room, he reviewed CCTV footage and crowd management arrangements across the mela area and directed officials to respond promptly to complaints and information received there.Inspecting the VIP parking area near the cremation ground, Shubhankar instructed officials to prevent unnecessary vehicle parking to ensure smooth pedestrian movement.He said the large influx of pilgrims from across India and abroad required coordinated efforts by all departments to provide a safe, clean and orderly environment.Meanwhile, Gaya Municipal Corporation showered flower petals on devotees using a drone at Vishnupad Temple, Falgu river and Dev Ghat on Monday as a gesture of welcome.A large number of pilgrims performed pinddaan on the 10th day of Gaya Shraddha at Gayakup and Gayasir pind vedis, besides Falgu river, Vishnupad Temple and Akshayvat.Senior Gayapal panda Gajadhar Lal Katariyar said pinddaan at Gaya is believed to help ancestors attain salvation. “The ritual holds special significance here, and pilgrims are advised to perform pind daan at these vedis as prescribed on Ashwin Krishna Dashami,” he said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news.
